curation_criteria: ICP-relevant frameworks only. Cut: ai-prompting, ai-architecture (non-business), ai-evaluation (non-business), ai-governance (non-strategic). ICP: tech founders, AI consultants, SMB leaders navigating tech disruption.

frameworks.name: Middleware Trap Diagnostic
frameworks.description: A five-step structured test to determine whether an AI company's position is structurally durable or merely renting its place in the stack by mapping dependencies and evaluating each against hyperscaler absorption risk.
when_to_apply: Our main model provider just announced features that overlap with our core product and I need to assess how exposed we are
I'm evaluating an AI startup for investment and need to determine if their defensibility is real or just a thin wrapper around someone else's capability
We build on top of a foundation model API and I need to present our board with an honest assessment of platform risk
Our differentiation story is 'domain expertise' but I'm not sure that holds up against what the big cloud providers are building
We need to decide whether to double down on our current stack position or pivot before a hyperscaler absorbs our layer
principles: If you don't own the layer below you or the customer relationship above you, you are borrowing time
Every dependency must be evaluated for both provider incentive and provider ability to absorb your functionality
Domain context claims must be stress-tested against the three-layer taxonomy before accepting them as moats
Analyze your position from the hyperscaler's perspective: do you generate more tokens for them, or sit between them and a customer they could serve directly?
The goal is to find positions where hyperscaler incentives align with your existence rather than your replacement
steps: Draw your stack: map every dependency your product requires — model, cloud, data sources, distribution channels
For each dependency, ask two questions: Does the provider have the incentive and ability to absorb my functionality? Is the provider now building the context layer I thought was my moat?

For each 'yes,' ask what you still own if that provider moves into your space — distinguish borrowed value (UX, integrations) from domain context, then classify that context using the three-layer test (structural, operational, or proprietary)

Check your remaining position against the four durable positions: proprietary context that can't rationally be platformized, infrastructure agents depend on, workflow depth with real switching costs, or trust and verification
Look at your position from the hyperscaler's perspective: does your existence generate more tokens for them, or do you sit between them and a customer they could serve directly at higher margin?

source_posts.title: Most AI companies are renting their position. These 4 prompts tell you if yours is one of them.

frameworks.example_application: The company's entire product sits on top of OpenAI's API, adds a fine-tuned workflow for legal contract review, and sells to mid-market law firms. Walking through the stack: model dependency is total (OpenAI), cloud is AWS, distribution is direct sales. OpenAI has both incentive and ability to build a legal template layer — they've already shipped custom GPTs. The claimed moat is 'we understand legal workflows,' but under the three-layer test, the context is structural (publicly available contract templates and clause libraries), not proprietary. What survives if OpenAI moves? The customer relationships with 200 law firms and 18 months of their marked-up clause data. That's real but thin — it's operational context at best, and the switching cost is low because firms haven't restructured their workflows around the tool. From the hyperscaler's perspective, this company sits directly between OpenAI and a high-value vertical they'd love to serve at higher margin. Verdict: this is a rented position with a 12-18 month window before absorption risk becomes acute.

frameworks.name: Three-Layer Enterprise Context Taxonomy
frameworks.description: A classification system that sorts enterprise domain context into three tiers — structural, operational, and proprietary — each with a distinct defensibility profile and recommended strategic response.
when_to_apply: We're deciding what enterprise data to share with our AI platform partner versus what to keep in-house
Our vertical AI startup claims 'domain expertise' as the moat — but I need to know how long that actually lasts as foundation models improve
A company in our portfolio says their institutional knowledge is their defensibility, but I suspect most of it is just system integration knowledge that platforms will absorb
We're negotiating a partnership with an AI infrastructure provider and need to know which data creates competitive exposure if shared
I'm trying to figure out whether our operational knowledge is actually proprietary or just not-yet-commoditized
principles: Structural context (system connections, permissions, data locations) is commodity plumbing that platform providers absorb within 12–24 months

Operational context defensibility is determined by rate of change: slowly-updating operational knowledge loses its window within one to two model generations; rapidly-updating knowledge stays defensible longer
Proprietary context (data and judgment that exists nowhere else and would create competitive exposure if shared) is the only tier worth defending as a strategic moat
Platforming proprietary context means giving the provider access to the thing that makes you competitively unique — today that is a partnership, in future model generations it may not be

source_posts.title: Most AI companies are renting their position. These 4 prompts tell you if yours is one of them.

frameworks.example_application: The company's claimed moat is 'deep understanding of healthcare billing workflows' — but decomposed through the taxonomy, most of that is structural context (which EHR systems connect to which clearinghouses, permission models, data locations) that any platform provider will absorb once they ship native integrations. The operational knowledge — billing code selection heuristics, denial pattern recognition — updates slowly enough that it's one model generation from commoditization. The only genuinely proprietary tier is their accumulated dataset of 200,000 real denial-overturn outcomes paired with the clinical judgment calls that drove them. That dataset exists nowhere else and would create competitive exposure if shared with a model provider. Strategic response: platform the structural and slow-updating operational layers freely, but the denial-overturn dataset is the thing worth defending — and platforming it means handing the model provider the one asset that makes the company irreplaceable.

frameworks.name: Four Durable Positions Framework
frameworks.description: A classification of the four AI stack positions where non-hyperscaler companies can build structurally durable businesses because the hyperscalers' incentives align with their existence rather than their replacement.
when_to_apply: Our product works today but I keep worrying that OpenAI or Google will just build this into their platform next quarter
We're an AI startup trying to decide which layer of the stack to build our core product around for long-term defensibility
Evaluating whether a portfolio company's AI positioning survives the next two rounds of platform consolidation
We've been told we're in the middleware trap and need to figure out which adjacent durable position to migrate toward
A founder is pitching us on AI infrastructure — how do I tell if their position gets stronger or weaker as the hyperscalers advance?
principles: Position 1 (Proprietary Context): Survive only in the proprietary context tier — structural and slowly-changing operational context will be absorbed by platform providers
Position 2 (Agent Infrastructure): Becoming a service that agents call regardless of who wins the orchestration war is more durable than competing in orchestration directly

Position 3 (Workflow Depth): Integration depth that encodes institutional workflows creates switching costs the model provider cannot easily replicate — value a product that gets harder to remove over time, not just better to use
Position 4 (Trust and Verification): The governance gap between agent capability adoption and auditability is the largest currently unoccupied structural position in the stack
Companies should target one of these four positions; straddling exposed middleware while also holding a durable position (as a search-augmented model does) creates asymmetric risk

source_posts.title: Most AI companies are renting their position. These 4 prompts tell you if yours is one of them.

frameworks.example_application: This compliance automation startup sits in Position 4 — Trust and Verification. Every time a hyperscaler ships more powerful agents, the governance gap widens, which increases demand for independent audit infrastructure. Their position strengthens as the platforms advance, which is the defining test of structural durability. By contrast, their competitor building a 'smart orchestration layer' is in exposed middleware — when Anthropic or OpenAI ships native multi-step tool use, that orchestration value collapses. The competitor should pivot toward encoding customer-specific compliance workflows (Position 3) or building the verification layer agents must call regardless of orchestrator (Position 2).

frameworks.name: AI Agent Supervision Model
frameworks.description: Reframes the role of a non-engineer using AI coding agents from 'prompter' to 'foreman'—shifting the key skill from clear description to active supervision with defined operational habits.
when_to_apply: My AI coding agent keeps breaking things I already had working and I don't know how to prevent it
I'm a non-technical founder using Cursor/Replit agents and I feel like I'm losing control of my codebase
I want to know the difference between getting better at prompting vs. getting better at managing AI agents
My vibe-coded app works for me but I'm nervous about whether it's actually safe for real users
I need to decide whether to keep building with AI agents myself or hire an engineer
principles: The shift from chat-based AI to agentic AI changes the primary skill from 'describe clearly' to 'supervise effectively'
You don't need to know the trade work; you need judgment about what's happening and when to stop
Five supervisory habits cover the majority of preventable disasters: version control, context management, rules files, blast radius control, and proactive quality demands
Bringing in an engineer is not failure—it is a transition point after demand is proven
Interrupting an agent is not rude; it is the job
The gap between 'works for me' and 'works for customers' requires proactive demands the agent will never raise unprompted

source_posts.title: Your AI coding agent deleted 2.5 years of customer data in minutes. Here's why an experienced engineer couldn't stop it — and the 5 habits that would have + 5 prompts.

frameworks.example_application: The conventional framing is that non-technical builders need to get better at prompting — describe what you want more precisely and the agent will build it right. That's wrong once you're using agentic AI. The real failure mode isn't imprecise instructions; it's unsupervised execution. The builder whose agent deleted 2.5 years of customer data wasn't bad at prompting — they were absent from supervision. The shift is from 'writer giving notes' to 'foreman on a job site': you need version control before every major change (so you can roll back), context management across sessions (so the agent doesn't lose the plot), rules files that encode past mistakes (so the agent doesn't repeat them), blast radius control (so one bad run can't destroy everything), and proactive quality demands (because the agent will never volunteer 'this isn't production-ready'). Knowing when to bring in a real engineer isn't failure — it's the sign that demand is proven and the project has graduated.

frameworks.name: Coordination Tax Audit
frameworks.description: A structured calendar analysis that categorizes all work hours into three buckets—coordination overhead, verifiable execution, and genuine residual judgment—to calculate the fraction of a role that is automatable or already obsolete.
when_to_apply: I spend most of my week in meetings and writing documents but I can't point to what I actually created
We're planning which team functions to hand off to AI agents and need a principled way to prioritize
My role feels important but I suspect most of what I do is just moving information between people who should already have it
I want a concrete, calendar-based measurement of how much of my job is automatable versus genuinely irreplaceable
We're restructuring headcount and need something more rigorous than gut feel about which roles are at risk
principles: Work hours fall into exactly three categories: coordination (meetings, translation artifacts, state synchronization), verifiable execution (tasks agents can already do or will within 18 months), and the genuine residual (zero-to-one judgment, political navigation, moral judgment, aesthetic taste).

The coordination category exists not because the work is inherently valuable, but because human bandwidth and context limits create a translation problem that would disappear if everyone shared perfect context.
What feels like 'judgment' is usually a composite of verifiable preparation work plus a thin layer of genuine non-verifiable judgment on top—the audit separates these.
Use the actual calendar from the prior week, not the idealized job description, as the data source.
The residual is what matters: identify what your role would look like if the coordination tax dropped to zero, then build a migration sequence for delegating coordination tasks to agents.
steps: Pull up your calendar from last week—the actual version, not the idealized one.

Count hours where the primary purpose was transferring information from someone who had it to someone who needed it (status updates, syncs, standups, one-on-ones for context transfer)—label these 'coordination.'

Count hours spent creating artifacts whose primary purpose was translating your knowledge into a form someone else could act on (PRDs, specs, briefs, decks, tickets, handoff documents)—also label these 'coordination.'

Count hours spent doing the thing you were actually hired to do—creating something that didn't exist before—label these as either 'verifiable execution' (testable, measurable output) or 'genuine residual' (non-verifiable judgment, vision, or insight).
Calculate your personal coordination tax percentage and compare it to the 60–70% benchmark.
From the residual bucket, map what your role would look like if you spent 30 hours per week on it instead of your current allocation.
Identify which coordination tasks are ready for agent delegation now, which need a verification layer first, and what the handoff protocol looks like for each—producing a concrete migration sequence.

source_posts.title: 80 out of every 200 employees exist to manage handoffs that agents are eliminating + the coordination tax audit to find yours
My honest field notes on scaling agents past the demo phase + 6 rules from teams running hundreds

frameworks.example_application: Last week's calendar shows 42 hours logged. 14 hours were meetings whose sole purpose was transferring context between people who didn't share it — standups, cross-team syncs, the Monday status review. Another 12 hours went to translation artifacts: writing a PRD that reformatted engineering context for a product review, updating tickets so another team could pick up work, building a deck that restated what was already in Slack threads. That's 26 hours — 62% — pure coordination tax, right at the benchmark. Of the remaining 16 hours, 11 were verifiable execution (drafting copy, building a prototype, running analysis) that an agent handles today with a verification layer. The genuine residual is 5 hours: deciding which market to enter, navigating a political conflict between two VPs, and making an aesthetic call on brand direction. The migration sequence starts with the translation artifacts — the PRD and ticket-writing are agent-ready now with a human review checkpoint.

frameworks.name: Double Compression Loop
frameworks.description: Challenges the standard 'AI automates X% of tasks' forecast by arguing that reducing human headcount makes remaining work more verifiable, which in turn expands what agents can handle—creating a compounding loop that makes static task-percentage models systematically undercount displacement.
when_to_apply: An analyst says AI will automate X% of jobs in our industry and I suspect that underestimates what actually happens
We're planning our automation roadmap and need to understand why the second and third rounds of displacement will be faster than the first
Leadership is treating AI adoption as a one-time headcount reduction rather than a compounding structural change
Our workforce planning model assumes the org chart stays roughly the same shape with fewer people in each box
We're debating whether coordination-heavy roles are safe from automation because they involve 'human judgment'
principles: The current distribution of tasks in an organization is not a natural set of things that need to be done—it is an artifact of human coordination requirements.
Reducing human headcount does not just eliminate coordination roles; it simultaneously makes remaining work more machine-inspectable and testable (more verifiable), expanding what agents can handle.
The loop compounds: fewer humans → less coordination → fewer coordination roles → remaining work more verifiable → agents handle more → fewer humans still.
Standard forecast models are wrong by design because they treat the task distribution as fixed; the distribution itself changes when the org structure changes.
Work expressed as code or code-like artifacts (machine-inspectable, testable) is the key threshold that determines agent eligibility.

source_posts.title: 80 out of every 200 employees exist to manage handoffs that agents are eliminating + the coordination tax audit to find yours

frameworks.example_application: A consulting firm's forecast says AI will automate 30% of a 200-person department's tasks. That number is wrong because it treats the current task distribution as fixed. Forty of those 200 people exist primarily to manage handoffs, approvals, and coordination between the other 160. When the first wave of automation removes 30 roles, the coordination load drops disproportionately — eliminating the need for another 15 coordination roles that weren't in the original automation scope. Simultaneously, the remaining work becomes more machine-inspectable (fewer handoff artifacts, more codified processes), which pushes the verifiability threshold down and makes a second wave of agent-eligible work appear that didn't exist in the original task inventory. The real displacement number isn't 30% — it's 55-65%, and it arrives in two compressed waves rather than one.

frameworks.name: Genuine Judgment vs. Coordination Overhead Disguised as Judgment
frameworks.description: Separates true non-verifiable judgment (conviction, empathy, structural bets with long-latency feedback) from complex coordination overhead that merely feels like judgment because it involves synthesis of many inputs—arguing the latter is automatable once verifiability barriers are removed.
when_to_apply: Someone argues a senior role is safe from AI because it requires 'strategic judgment' or 'years of experience'
We're designing human-agent task splits and struggling to decide what stays with the human versus what gets delegated
A domain like brand strategy or investment selection is claimed to be inherently subjective and unmeasurable
Leadership is resisting automation of a function because the work 'requires synthesis that only a human can do'
We need to figure out which parts of an executive's week are genuinely irreplaceable versus expensive coordination overhead
principles: Most 'judgment-heavy' roles are composites: a large layer of verifiable preparation work plus a thin layer of genuine non-verifiable judgment on top.
The verifiability barrier in many 'judgment' domains is not the nature of the decision itself but the opacity of the decision process—agent harnesses make reasoning inspectable.

True non-verifiable judgment has long-latency feedback (outcomes only apparent years later), involves commitments that constrain future optionality, or requires non-dataset context such as empathy or political navigation.
Work bundled as 'one role does both' was organizationally efficient, not structurally indivisible—agent harnesses unbundle preparation from judgment.
The test: could the outcome be measured against data if the feedback loop were faster and cleaner? If yes, it is verifiable preparation masquerading as judgment.

source_posts.title: 80 out of every 200 employees exist to manage handoffs that agents are eliminating + the coordination tax audit to find yours

frameworks.example_application: The VP of Pricing claims their work is pure judgment — reading the market, sensing customer willingness to pay, making calls competitors can't replicate. But decomposing the role reveals that 80% of the time goes to synthesizing competitor pricing data, segmenting customers by usage patterns, and modeling elasticity scenarios — all verifiable against revenue outcomes within a quarter. The genuine judgment layer is thin: it's the decision to hold price during a downturn when the board is panicking, a commitment that constrains future positioning and won't show results for 18 months. The synthesis work feels like judgment because it requires holding many inputs simultaneously, but faster feedback loops and agent harnesses make it inspectable and automatable. The role should be unbundled: agent-driven pricing analysis with a human retaining only the conviction-level strategic bets.

frameworks.name: Capability-Dissipation Gap
frameworks.description: A framework that maps the widening distance between what AI can technically do (capability curve) and what the economy has actually reorganized around AI doing (dissipation curve), explaining why both doom and boom AI narratives are wrong about timing and why the gap itself creates asymmetric economic opportunity for early adopters.
when_to_apply: Markets just sold off on an AI disruption headline and I need to decide if it's signal or timeline confusion
I'm a small team wondering whether our AI adoption advantage will last or if big competitors will catch up within months
Someone is arguing that AI will either destroy all jobs soon or that it's overhyped — and I suspect both takes are wrong in the same way
I'm deciding how much to invest in reorganizing my workflow around AI now versus waiting for the tools to mature
Leadership is asking whether our AI pilot needs to scale company-wide immediately or whether a phased approach still captures most of the value
principles: AI capability compounds faster than societal dissipation; the gap between the two curves is the primary variable most analyses ignore
The gap is maintained by four inertia forces: regulatory, organizational, cultural, and trust drag
A wide gap creates asymmetric returns for early adopters precisely because uniform adoption would eliminate the advantage
Large firms have capital and data advantages but carry full organizational inertia; small firms and individuals have speed advantages and lighter inertia
The gap erodes slowly, meaning early-adoption advantages persist and compound longer than conventional models predict
Both doom and boom narratives are internally flawed in the same way: they assume the gap closes fast

source_posts.title: The economist who formalized the AI doom scenario says its own conditions are too extreme to hold — here's what the math actually shows + the gap framework that changes your career calculus

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that large incumbents will quickly absorb AI and neutralize any startup or individual advantage. That's wrong here because the dissipation curve — how fast organizations actually reorganize around new capability — is governed by regulatory, organizational, cultural, and trust drag, all of which large firms carry in full. A three-person team adopting AI coding tools today isn't just 'early' — their advantage compounds for as long as the gap stays wide, and the gap stays wide far longer than disruption narratives assume. The doom scenario (mass displacement next year) and the boom scenario (every company AI-native by 2026) both fail for the same reason: they treat the capability curve as the dissipation curve. The actual opportunity is in the widening space between the two, where returns to early adopters are asymmetric precisely because most of the economy hasn't reorganized yet.

frameworks.name: Four Forms of Societal Inertia
frameworks.description: A classification of the four distinct drag forces that slow translation of AI capability into economic impact — regulatory, organizational, cultural, and trust inertia — each with different drivers, timelines, and implications for adoption strategy.
when_to_apply: We have an AI tool that clearly works, but our enterprise customers keep saying 'not yet' and I can't figure out what's actually blocking them
I'm building a deployment timeline for AI in a regulated industry and need to know which bottlenecks will dominate
A competitor claims they'll have AI deployed across their org in six months — is that credible given how these institutions actually work?
Our pilot went great but scaling across the organization has stalled for reasons that seem to shift every time we ask
I need to explain to investors why AI-driven productivity gains won't show up in our sector's economics for several years
principles: Regulatory inertia: rules, procurement cycles, and compliance requirements (HIPAA, FDA, etc.) impose delays measured in years, not quarters
Organizational inertia: headcount and workflow decisions are filtered through HR policy, employment law, management politics, and institutional knowledge concerns — not pure efficiency logic
Cultural inertia: adoption curves lag capability curves even in technically sophisticated organizations; behavior change requires mandates, incentives, and deliberate skill-building
Trust inertia: enterprises require verification infrastructure, audit trails, and liability frameworks before deploying AI at scale — capability benchmarks cannot compress this timeline
All four forces operate simultaneously and compound each other, making the aggregate drag much larger than any single force

source_posts.title: The economist who formalized the AI doom scenario says its own conditions are too extreme to hold — here's what the math actually shows + the gap framework that changes your career calculus

frameworks.example_application: A health-tech startup's AI diagnostic tool outperforms radiologists on benchmarks, but hospital adoption is stalling. The binding constraint isn't cultural or organizational — radiology departments are eager and technically ready. The dominant inertia is regulatory (FDA clearance timelines, HIPAA compliance infrastructure) compounded by trust inertia (hospitals require audit trails, liability frameworks, and malpractice insurance clarity before deploying at scale). Organizational and cultural inertia are secondary here. This means the adoption timeline is gated by regulatory cycles measured in years, and no amount of internal change management or capability demonstration compresses it. The startup's go-to-market should target the regulatory and trust layers directly — pursue FDA breakthrough designation and build verification infrastructure — rather than investing in more clinical champions or training programs.

frameworks.name: Distillation as Piracy (Reframe)
frameworks.description: Reframes AI capability extraction from a geopolitical/espionage problem into an information economics problem analogous to digital piracy, which changes the predicted trajectory and appropriate response.
when_to_apply: A cheap open-source model just matched our frontier performance and we're trying to figure out how
We're debating whether export controls on AI chips and model weights will actually prevent capability transfer
Our competitive strategy assumes our model capability lead will last 18+ months
Policy team is framing AI capability leakage as an espionage problem requiring intelligence-community solutions
We're a non-hyperscaler AI lab deciding whether to open-source or keep our model weights proprietary
principles: AI capabilities are stored as math — weightless, copyable, extractable through a chat window — making them more like music files than nuclear material
When extraction costs thousands and independent development costs billions, the information always moves — not from malice but from overwhelming economics
The correct question about an impressive cheap model is not 'how did they do it so cheaply?' but 'what fraction was independently developed?'
Piracy doesn't stop — it slows down; every safeguard is a speed bump, and speed bumps matter because capability curves are exponential
The incentive to distill is universal, not China-specific — any non-hyperscaler faces the same pressure gradient
A time lead, not permanent exclusivity, is the realistic competitive advantage; invest in speed bumps accordingly

source_posts.title: 16 million stolen conversations, 24,000 fake accounts, and what it means for the AI tools you're choosing this week + the manifold probe

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read on DeepSeek R1 is espionage — stolen secrets, state-backed theft. That framing is wrong because it predicts the wrong countermeasures. AI capabilities are weightless math extractable through a chat window; when independent development costs billions and distillation costs thousands, the information moves regardless of who's doing it. Every non-hyperscaler on earth faces the same pressure gradient — this isn't a China problem, it's a piracy problem. The realistic play isn't permanent exclusivity (that's the RIAA suing Napster); it's investing in speed bumps that preserve a time lead, because on an exponential capability curve, even six months of delay changes who captures the value.

frameworks.name: Three Missing Layers of Organizational AI Architecture
frameworks.description: A three-layer diagnostic framework identifying the structural gaps that prevent AI deployments from delivering organizational value: unified context infrastructure, coherent AI workflow architecture, and organizational intent alignment.
when_to_apply: Every team has their own AI tools but nothing connects and we're not seeing enterprise-level impact
Our AI agents are making decisions that are technically correct but strategically wrong — they don't seem to understand our priorities
We ran successful AI pilots in three departments but the enterprise-wide rollout stalled and nobody can explain why
We're trying to figure out why individual AI fluency isn't translating into organizational productivity gains
We need to design the AI infrastructure for a new organization or audit why our existing architecture isn't delivering value
principles: Layer One (Unified Context Infrastructure): agents need a single, governed, cross-departmental context stack — not team-by-team RAG pipelines
Layer Two (Coherent AI Worker Toolkit): individual AI fluency must ladder into shared organizational infrastructure to produce leverage beyond individual tasks

Layer Three (Organizational Alignment / Intent Engineering): human-readable OKRs and principles must be decomposed into agent-actionable decision boundaries, escalation triggers, value hierarchies, and feedback loops
Skipping any layer creates the intent gap: tools deployed without infrastructure become expensive toys
The context infrastructure question is architectural and political, not primarily technical
Agents need explicit alignment before they start working, not absorbed gradually through osmosis like human employees

source_posts.title: Klarna saved $60 million and broke its company. The missing layer is what I'm calling intent engineering + 2 prompts to find yours

frameworks.example_application: This organization has Layer One missing. Every department built its own RAG pipeline — sales has one over CRM data, support has one over tickets, product has one over Jira. But no agent can answer 'what did the customer who filed this support ticket buy, what feature did they request in their last sales call, and is that on the roadmap?' The context is balkanized, so agents optimize locally and contradict each other across departments. The fix isn't better prompts or smarter models — it's a unified context infrastructure that is as much a political negotiation about data governance as it is a technical project. Until that exists, Layer Two and Three investments will produce expensive toys.

frameworks.name: AI Succeeds at the Wrong Thing
frameworks.description: Reframes AI deployment failures not as technology failures but as intent failures — the AI worked exactly as designed, optimizing for a measurable proxy while destroying the unmeasured organizational goal it was supposed to serve.
when_to_apply: Our AI system is performing well on every dashboard metric but stakeholders are increasingly unhappy with outcomes
Leadership is blaming model quality for a deployment that technically works but produces bad business results
We automated a human workflow and the measurable outputs improved but something intangible got worse
An AI agent completed tasks correctly but caused unexpected downstream problems in other parts of the organization
We're debating whether to upgrade our model when the real issue might be what we told it to optimize for
principles: AI that fails and AI that succeeds at the wrong thing are different problems requiring different solutions
Measurable objectives are proxies for organizational intent, not the intent itself — optimizing proxies can destroy the underlying goal
Human employees absorb unmeasured organizational values through osmosis; agents cannot and will not
The question is not 'can AI do this task?' but 'can AI do this task in a way that serves our organizational goals?'
Model quality is rarely the bottleneck; organizational intent alignment almost always is

source_posts.title: Klarna saved $60 million and broke its company. The missing layer is what I'm calling intent engineering + 2 prompts to find yours

frameworks.example_application: Klarna's AI customer service agent resolved 2.3 million conversations and saved $60 million — those are the metrics it was optimized for. But resolution speed and cost reduction are proxies for customer satisfaction and brand trust, not the thing itself. Human agents absorbed unstated organizational values — empathy during billing disputes, judgment about when to escalate, awareness that a frustrated customer's lifetime value dwarfs the cost of a longer call. The AI optimized the proxy perfectly and destroyed the unmeasured goal. The failure isn't that the technology wasn't ready; it's that the organization never translated its actual intent into something the system could optimize for.

frameworks.name: Six Axes of Hard (Work Difficulty Decomposition Framework)
frameworks.description: A six-category classification system for identifying what actually makes a piece of work difficult, enabling more precise AI tool selection and career risk assessment by matching each difficulty type to its automation timeline.
when_to_apply: I tried using AI on a task and it didn't help, but I can't explain why it fell short
I'm trying to figure out which parts of my job are safe from automation and which aren't
We're selecting AI tools for different parts of a workflow and need a principled way to route tasks
A project keeps stalling despite having smart people and good tools — something about the difficulty isn't being addressed
I need to explain to my team why some knowledge work automates easily while other work that seems similar doesn't
principles: 'Hard' is not a single dimension — conflating different types of difficulty leads to wrong tool choices and career misjudgments
Each axis has a different automation timeline and is addressed by different AI capabilities
Reasoning problems (novel multi-step logical deduction) are a relatively narrow slice of most knowledge work, despite dominating AI benchmark discourse
Effort and coordination problems are the dominant axes for most daily knowledge work and are being automated by agentic AI now
Emotional intelligence, judgment/willpower, and ambiguity resolution are the last axes to yield to AI and represent the most durable human value
Identify the bottleneck axis first before selecting a tool — the gap is usually in how the problem is framed, not which model is used
Domain expertise problems sit between — models simulate it via training data but the 'has lived it' gap remains real
steps: Identify a specific task or role component to analyze

Classify its primary difficulty axis: Reasoning (novel multi-step logical deduction), Effort (large surface area requiring sustained thoroughness), Coordination (aligning people/teams/information flows), Emotional Intelligence (reading and responding to human dynamics), Judgment/Willpower (courage to act on the right answer despite cost), Domain Expertise (pattern recognition from accumulated experience), or Ambiguity (defining what the question even is)
Identify the bottleneck axis — the one dimension that, if solved, would unlock the most progress

Map the bottleneck axis to its current AI automation status: Reasoning and Effort axes are being automated rapidly now; Coordination is beginning to yield; Domain Expertise is slowly being absorbed; Emotional Intelligence, Judgment, and Ambiguity are barely touched
Select AI tooling matched to the bottleneck axis, or accept that human judgment is still required if the bottleneck is on the last three axes
Reassess periodically as the automation timeline for each axis advances

source_posts.title: The 6 reasons your work is hard — and which ones AI is automating this year + prompts to build your map

frameworks.example_application: This product manager's role looks like it should be heavily automated — there's research synthesis, roadmap writing, stakeholder updates. But the bottleneck axis isn't reasoning or effort, it's ambiguity resolution: the hardest part is figuring out what the right question even is when the CEO, engineering lead, and top customer each frame the problem differently. That axis is barely touched by current AI. The effort axis (compiling competitive intel, drafting specs) is fully automatable now and should be delegated immediately, but the role itself stays durable as long as the ambiguity and judgment axes remain the actual bottleneck.

frameworks.name: Three Developer Tracks
frameworks.description: Classifies the diverging developer career paths in the AI era into three distinct roles with different skill requirements, compensation dynamics, and career trajectories.
when_to_apply: I'm a mid-career developer and I'm not sure if I should go deeper into systems work or lean into my industry knowledge
My team has developers whose roles are becoming redundant as AI handles more routine coding — how do I restructure around what's left?
I've been a competent generalist programmer for years and I'm starting to feel like that's not enough anymore
We're rewriting job descriptions for software roles and the old 'software engineer' title doesn't capture the diverging skill sets we actually need
I have domain expertise in a specific industry but I've always thought of myself as 'just a developer' — is that expertise actually my main asset now?
principles: The binary 'AI replaces developers or it doesn't' framing is useless; role differentiation is the real story
The middle of the old distribution — competent generalist coders without deep systems or domain expertise — is most exposed
Each track has different value drivers: Orchestrators scale with token budgets, Systems Builders scale with infrastructure leverage, Domain Translators scale with niche specificity
Cheaper intelligence increases the value of Domain Translators by making more niche problems economically viable to solve
Decisive movement toward one track is preferable to staying in the generic middle
steps: Identify which track aligns with existing strengths: problem decomposition and specification (Orchestrator), deep systems and probabilistic infrastructure work (Systems Builder), or domain expertise combined with AI fluency (Domain Translator)
Assess current position relative to the 'exposed middle' — generic application code production without deep specialization in either direction
Build skills and positioning toward the chosen track
For Orchestrators: develop system design, specification writing, quality evaluation, and token economics skills
For Systems Builders: develop mechanical understanding of model behavior, context window dynamics, and reliable system design on probabilistic components
For Domain Translators: deepen vertical market knowledge and acquire minimum viable AI fluency to direct intelligence at domain-specific problems

source_posts.title: OpenAI is charging $20K/month for an AI employee — and enterprise buyers think it's cheap

frameworks.example_application: This developer has eight years of full-stack experience building CRUD apps and API integrations — competent, productive, but no deep systems expertise and no domain specialization. That's the exposed middle: the exact work AI handles fastest and cheapest. The strongest existing asset is three years building healthcare compliance tools — that's a Domain Translator seed. The move is to deepen healthcare regulatory knowledge and pair it with AI fluency, not to compete on raw code output where the floor is collapsing. Staying a 'good generalist' is the highest-risk position in the current market.

frameworks.name: Distribution Beats Compute
frameworks.description: Reframes AI competition away from token volume and capital as the primary axis, arguing that when intelligence is commoditized, competitive advantage migrates to distribution, domain expertise, and customer relationships that capital cannot replicate.
when_to_apply: We're a small team and a big player just launched something that overlaps with our AI product — should we pivot or double down?
I'm a domain expert considering building an AI product in my field, but I don't have the compute budget that tech companies have
An investor is telling me my vertical AI company's TAM is too small because they're sizing it against SaaS benchmarks instead of labor replacement
Our startup is debating whether to go horizontal to capture more market or stay focused on one industry vertical
I'm evaluating whether a vertical AI company has a real moat or just a head start that evaporates when GPT gets better
principles: Enterprises will always win on raw token volume — competing on inference spend is a losing strategy for smaller players

When the core input (intelligence) is commoditized, competitive advantage migrates to everything surrounding it: distribution, domain knowledge, customer relationships, proprietary data, workflow integration, trust
The intelligence is purchasable; the channel never will be
Vertical AI addresses labor and services spend, not just software license spend — making TAMs appear larger than legacy SaaS analysis suggests
Precise aim with limited resources beats large budgets pointed at the wrong problem
Knowing your customer beats knowing your API

source_posts.title: OpenAI is charging $20K/month for an AI employee — and enterprise buyers think it's cheap

frameworks.example_application: A three-person team building AI-powered compliance tooling for community banks is worried about competing with a well-funded horizontal AI platform. The conventional read is that the big player's $200M inference budget makes them unbeatable. That's wrong here — community bank compliance officers don't need more intelligence, they need intelligence that already understands their regulatory context, speaks their language, and integrates into their existing workflows. The big platform has to serve thousands of use cases generically; the small team's six months of embedded domain relationships and purpose-built workflows represent distribution and trust that no amount of compute spend can replicate. The intelligence is purchasable at commodity rates; the channel into 5,000 community banks never will be.

frameworks.name: Three Categories of AI Exposure
frameworks.description: A classification system that sorts industries or business models into three tiers based on the actual timing and severity of AI disruption risk, enabling investors and strategists to distinguish genuine near-term threats from overstated or distant ones.
when_to_apply: A sector just sold off 15-20% on AI disruption fears and I need to figure out if it's a buying opportunity or the market finally catching up
My company's board is demanding an urgent AI transformation plan because our stock dropped, but I'm not sure the threat is actually near-term
I'm comparing two investment targets in different industries that have both been penalized equally for AI exposure, and that feels wrong
A competitor announced an AI product that does part of what we do, and I need to gauge whether this is an existential threat or a feature demo
I'm allocating R&D budget between defending against AI disruption and growing the core business, and I need to know how urgent the defensive spend actually is
principles: Not all industries face AI disruption on the same timeline; treat them differently
Category 1 (immediate displacement): AI is genuinely displacing labor now — per-seat software models, routine code generation, and similar work are being disrupted in real time

Category 2 (medium-term transition): AI will matter on a 3-to-5-year horizon but current panic vastly overstates near-term risk — relationship-based services like wealth management and commercial insurance brokerage fall here

Category 3 (market has lost the plot): AI disruption is theoretically probable but the timeline being priced is delusional — industries with deep proprietary data, complex physical/regulatory operations, or entrenched relationships fall here
The market pricing all three categories identically is the error — and that mispricing creates both investment opportunity and strategic misdirection
Distinguish between 'disruption is probable' and 'disruption is imminent'; the market conflates these

source_posts.title: A $3 million karaoke company just triggered a global logistics selloff + the 3 categories that tell you whether to panic or buy

frameworks.example_application: A commercial insurance brokerage trading at 8x earnings after an AI-fear selloff is a Category 3 mispricing. The business runs on decades of proprietary claims data, entrenched carrier relationships, and regulatory complexity that no AI system can shortcut in under five years. The market is pricing it as if GPT-5 replaces the entire distribution chain next quarter. Meanwhile, a per-seat SaaS tool for boilerplate legal document review is genuine Category 1 — the displacement is measurable right now in lost renewals, and the stock decline reflects reality, not panic.

frameworks.name: Building vs. Buying AI Response
frameworks.description: A diagnostic distinction that separates companies genuinely integrating AI into workflows (builders) from companies announcing AI partnerships for investor optics (buyers), used to assess whether an organization's AI response will create durable competitive advantage or just a press release.
when_to_apply: A company I'm evaluating just announced a big AI partnership right after a stock drop — is this real or panic spending?
I need to figure out whether my employer's AI reorganization will make us stronger or is just theater for the board
An enterprise customer is claiming they're 'AI-first' now and I need to assess whether they'll actually integrate or just bolt on a vendor
I'm advising a board that wants to respond to AI disruption pressure and I need to distinguish genuine investment from reactive spending
Two competitors both announced AI strategies — how do I tell which one will actually compound and which is performative?
principles: Net-new investment layered on top of existing capabilities signals genuine positioning for the transition
AI budget cannibalized from product, engineering, or core domain teams signals optimization for investor narrative rather than competitive advantage
Builders develop compounding advantages with every model upgrade; buyers get a vendor logo on a slide deck
The gap between these two responses becomes visible in every metric that matters within 12 months
Defensive AI postures adopted under stock pressure often make companies more vulnerable to actual disruption later

source_posts.title: A $3 million karaoke company just triggered a global logistics selloff + the 3 categories that tell you whether to panic or buy

frameworks.example_application: This company announced a $200M 'AI transformation' two weeks after their stock dropped 18% on disruption fears. The tell: the AI budget was carved from their core engineering and product teams, not layered on top. They're buying, not building. In 12 months, they'll have a partnership logo on their investor deck and fewer engineers who understand their own product. Meanwhile, their competitor quietly hired 40 ML engineers funded by new budget and is retraining models on proprietary logistics data — that's the builder, and the gap between them will be irreversible by Q3.

frameworks.name: The Five Levels of Vibe Coding
frameworks.description: A six-tier classification system (Level 0–5) that maps where a developer or team actually stands in their AI-assisted development practice, from line-by-line autocomplete to fully autonomous software factories.
when_to_apply: My team uses Copilot and Cursor daily but I'm not sure we're actually getting the productivity gains we should be
We're evaluating an 'agentic coding' tool that claims to handle full features autonomously — how do I assess whether that's real?
I need to build an AI adoption roadmap for our engineering org and I don't know what the actual milestones look like
Developers on my team resist letting AI write whole features — they insist on reviewing every diff — and I'm trying to figure out if that's the right call or the bottleneck
We want to get to autonomous code generation but I don't know what organizational changes are required beyond just buying better tools
principles: Each level represents a fundamentally different human-AI relationship, not just a quantitative improvement in tool use
The bottleneck shifts at each level: from keystrokes (Level 0) to task scope (Level 1) to diff review (Level 2-3) to specification quality (Level 4-5)
Most self-identified 'AI-native' developers cluster at Level 2, not Level 3-5 where they believe they operate
Advancing beyond Level 3 requires organizational and psychological change, not just better tools
Level 5 requires that no human writes code and no human reviews code — the factory evaluates outcomes, not implementation
steps: Level 0 (Spicy Autocomplete): AI suggests next lines; human still writes all software
Level 1 (Coding Intern): AI handles discrete, well-scoped tasks; human reviews all output and retains architecture
Level 2 (Junior Developer): AI handles multi-file changes across a codebase; human reads every diff
Level 3 (Developer as Manager): Human directs AI and reviews output; AI does all implementation; human day is diffs
Level 4 (Developer as PM): Human writes a specification, leaves, returns to evaluate whether outcomes are correct; no diff reading
Level 5 (Dark Factory): Specification in, working software out; no human writes code, no human reviews code; humans approve outcomes only

source_posts.title: The dark factory is real, most developers are getting slower, and your org chart is the bottleneck (plus 5 prompts to get from level 2 to 5)

frameworks.example_application: This team says they're 'fully AI-native' but every PR still gets a line-by-line human diff review and developers manually architect all modules before handing tasks to Copilot. That's Level 2 — Junior Developer — not Level 4 where they claim to be. The tell is that the bottleneck is still diff-reading throughput, not specification quality. Moving to Level 3 requires the team to stop reading every line of generated code and start managing AI output the way a manager reviews a developer's work. That's a psychological shift — trusting outcomes over inspecting implementation — and no tool upgrade will get them there without it.

frameworks.name: Delegation Bet vs. Coordination Bet
frameworks.description: A distinction between two fundamentally different AI agent philosophies — autonomous delegation (hand off a task and walk away) versus integrated coordination (agents working inside existing tools and talking to each other) — that determines which organizational muscle to build.
when_to_apply: We're deciding between an autonomous coding agent like Codex and an integrated agent system like Claude with MCP — how do we choose?
Our AI agent deployment is producing good outputs but the team spends more time copy-pasting results between tools than they save
Leadership wants to adopt AI agents org-wide but different teams have fundamentally different workflow structures
We picked an AI agent platform six months ago and now switching feels impossibly expensive — was our initial choice wrong?
Should we invest in building agent-to-agent coordination infrastructure or just give each team member a powerful autonomous assistant?
principles: Delegation bet: one sufficiently capable agent working alone produces trusted output without supervision — value comes from correctness and autonomy
Coordination bet: real work is fundamentally interdependent and agents must talk to each other and integrate with existing tools — value comes from connectivity and coordination
The architectural starting point shapes every downstream feature, default, and assumption, making the approaches remain distinct even as they partially converge
Integration ecosystems compound via network effects — each new tool connection makes the whole system more useful — while isolated architectures do not benefit from this flywheel
The tool choice reshapes organizational structure (delegation culture vs. coordination culture), making switching later an operational restructuring rather than a software migration
Both patterns are valid; the error is applying the wrong pattern to a workflow, not choosing one over the other universally

source_posts.title: Codex 5.3 vs. Opus 4.6: Why your AI agent choice compounds faster than you think + the workflow audit that prevents the wrong one

frameworks.example_application: This team's work is fundamentally interdependent — a single research task touches the CRM, three Slack channels, a shared doc, and a project tracker before it's 'done.' That's a coordination bet, not a delegation bet. Deploying Codex-style autonomous agents here means the team will manually stitch outputs back into their tools, which is slower than the original workflow. The right move is an integration-first agent architecture where value compounds through connectivity — each new tool connection makes every workflow faster. Choosing the delegation path would feel productive for the first week and create operational drag for the next twelve months.

frameworks.name: Infrastructure Inversion Pattern
frameworks.description: A classification framework that identifies which position an entity occupies in a platform-building cycle—platform builder, defensible tenant, or vulnerable tenant—and predicts value capture based on whether the infrastructure being built is a 'dumb pipe' or an integrated intelligence layer.
when_to_apply: We're debating whether the massive AI infrastructure spending is a bubble or whether we should be investing even more aggressively
Our product is built on top of a foundation model API and I'm trying to figure out if we're building value or just renting someone else's platform
Should we build our own infrastructure layer now or wait until the technology matures and build applications on top of whoever wins?
I'm trying to understand why this technology investment cycle might play out differently from the dot-com fiber overbuild
Our board thinks we can catch up on AI infrastructure in 2-3 years — I need to explain why the window might already be closing
principles: Every major economic era begins with massive infrastructure overbuilding followed by investor panic before the infrastructure's true use is discovered
Infrastructure is never built for the thing that makes it valuable—it's built for what the builders imagine, then used for what the next generation imagines
Platform builders capture the economics of everything built on top; companies that wait become tenants paying the platform's margins
The structural difference between dumb-pipe infrastructure (railroads, fiber) and intelligent infrastructure (AI models) changes who captures downstream value
When infrastructure is vertically integrated with the intelligence it delivers, builders can capture application-layer value, not just hosting fees
The window for platform-building compresses with each successive infrastructure cycle: railroads took 20 years, fiber took 10, AWS took 6, AI is moving in ~18 months
The penalty for underbuilding in an infrastructure inversion is permanent—you cannot catch up after the window closes

source_posts.title: $185 billion is the down payment — the 4 skills that survive when agents code for months

frameworks.example_application: The $185 billion flowing into AI infrastructure isn't a bubble — it follows the same pattern as railroads, fiber optic, and cloud. But unlike fiber (a dumb pipe where the builders went bankrupt while Google and Netflix captured the value), AI infrastructure is vertically integrated with intelligence. The model builders aren't laying cable for someone else to use — they're building the intelligence layer itself, which means they capture application-layer economics too. A company building SaaS features on top of OpenAI's API is a vulnerable tenant: the platform builder can ship their feature as a checkbox. The 18-month window for establishing a defensible position — through proprietary data, workflow integration, or building your own infrastructure layer — is compressing faster than any prior cycle, and the penalty for waiting is permanent tenancy.

frameworks.name: Four Skills That Survive Infrastructure Inversion
frameworks.description: A rubric of four human capabilities—taste, exquisite domain judgment, phenomenal ramp, and relentless honesty about value migration—that retain or appreciate in value when AI agents automate execution-layer work.
when_to_apply: I'm trying to figure out where to invest my learning time when AI capabilities seem to shift every week
I spend most of my day on execution tasks and I'm starting to wonder if that's a career risk
We're hiring for a role that's going to be heavily augmented by AI agents — what should we screen for?
Someone on my team insists their value is in the craft of writing code, not in the judgment around what to build and why
I'm advising someone who wants to wait until AI 'stabilizes' before adapting their workflow
principles: Taste—the ability to distinguish competent from excellent output by hard-won instinct—becomes exponentially more valuable when the cost of generating options drops to zero
Exquisite domain judgment means specific, contextual, intuitive knowledge of how a domain actually works, accumulated through experience that cannot yet be replicated from training data
Phenomenal ramp is the meta-skill: the ability to absorb capability changes at speed so all other skills remain applicable as the frontier moves weekly
Relentless honesty about value migration requires actively inventorying which parts of your work are judgment versus execution and reallocating time before the market forces it
Most people's time allocation is inverted—they spend the majority of hours on execution skills that are depreciating fastest
Waiting for AI to 'settle down' before rebuilding professional infrastructure is equivalent to waiting for cloud to 'prove itself' in 2008—you pay a compounding learning-curve tax

source_posts.title: $185 billion is the down payment — the 4 skills that survive when agents code for months

frameworks.example_application: This senior engineer spends 70% of their time writing implementation code and 30% on architecture reviews and quality judgment calls. That ratio is inverted — the 70% is the fastest-depreciating slice of their portfolio. The architecture taste and domain judgment (knowing which database choice will cause pain at scale in this specific regulatory environment) are the appreciating assets. The immediate reallocation: shift to 30% execution / 70% judgment, using AI agents for the implementation layer, and invest freed hours into phenomenal ramp — staying current with how agent capabilities change the architecture options weekly. The fourth skill — relentless honesty about value migration — is the one that makes this reallocation happen at all, because without it, the engineer tells themselves 'I'm a better coder than any AI' and misses the window.

frameworks.name: Inference Gap Analysis
frameworks.description: A distinction between training-era and inference-era infrastructure economics that explains why bubble analyses built on training-cost math systematically underestimate agent-driven compute demand.
when_to_apply: I keep seeing analysts argue that AI infrastructure spending is a bubble — are they missing something?
We're trying to forecast compute costs for deploying autonomous agents across our enterprise and the numbers seem impossibly large
Why do AI infrastructure spending estimates keep getting revised upward every quarter?
Our capacity planning assumes chatbot-level inference loads but we're moving to agentic workflows — how far off are we?
Evaluating whether hyperscaler capex announcements are rational given current AI revenue
principles: Training compute is expensive but bursty and front-loaded; inference compute is cheaper per unit but continuous and scales with deployment
A human interacting with a chatbot generates modest inference load; an autonomous agent performing a workflow generates continuous inference at orders of magnitude higher volume
Agent workloads multiply inference demand across every enterprise workflow simultaneously, not just individual user sessions
Analysts who correctly called the bubble were analyzing training economics; they were wrong because the actual demand driver is inference for agents
The shift from training-era to inference-era spending makes previously 'excessive' capex numbers look undersized when modeled against agentic workloads

source_posts.title: $185 billion is the down payment — the 4 skills that survive when agents code for months

frameworks.example_application: The bearish thesis on $185B in AI capex looks airtight if you model training economics — training runs are bursty, front-loaded, and plateau once a model ships. But that's the wrong demand curve. A single enterprise deploying 10,000 autonomous agents running continuous multi-step workflows generates inference load that dwarfs anything a million chatbot users produce. The analysts who called it a bubble were right about training math and catastrophically wrong about which compute era we're entering. That $185B isn't excess — it's the down payment on inference infrastructure that doesn't exist yet.

frameworks.name: The 70/30 Rule for Human-Agent Delegation
frameworks.description: Reframes agent deployment design around the research-backed finding that people want 70% human control and 30% agent delegation, rather than the 0/100 full-autonomy architecture most agent systems default to.
when_to_apply: We built a fully autonomous agent workflow and adoption is much lower than expected despite strong capability metrics
Deciding how much autonomy to give an AI agent that handles tasks with social consequences like emails, calendar management, or client communication
Our team keeps manually overriding or ignoring the agent's outputs even though they're usually correct
Where exactly should I place human approval gates in an agentic workflow — I don't want to bottleneck everything but I can't let it run free
Planning a phased rollout of an AI agent and need to decide what to automate now versus what to keep human-controlled
principles: People will choose a less competent human helper over a more competent AI helper when stakes are real — this is psychological, not rational
Design for 70/30 by default: agent executes, human decides
Build approval gates so agents draft and humans send, agents research and humans decide, agents monitor and humans act
Trust is the actual bottleneck, not capability — governance must precede autonomy expansion
Increase delegation incrementally as operating history and trust accumulate, not based on capability alone

source_posts.title: 160,000 developers are building digital employees, not chatbots + the 4 prompts I use to deploy agents safely

frameworks.example_application: The conventional assumption is that the email-drafting agent should send autonomously because it achieves 95% quality parity with human-written emails. That's wrong here because the cost of a bad email is social and reputational — exactly the domain where people choose a less competent human over a more competent AI. The architecture should be agent-drafts, human-sends: the agent composes and suggests timing, but the send button stays with the person. Adoption will climb because the user feels control over the risk surface, and over three months of operating history with zero embarrassing sends, the approval gate can be relaxed to auto-send for routine confirmations while keeping human review on anything external or senior-facing.

frameworks.name: Network Intelligence Framework
frameworks.description: A six-part analytical system for evaluating professional network health and job-search readiness using exported LinkedIn data, classifying connections by relationship strength, reciprocity, advocacy likelihood, dormancy, archetype, and warm-path potential.
when_to_apply: I'm about to start a job search and I have no idea which of my 800 LinkedIn connections would actually help me
I need a warm intro to a specific company but I can't figure out who in my network is closest to them
I haven't talked to most of my professional contacts in years and I need to figure out which relationships are worth reviving
I need to pick references but I'm not sure who would actually advocate strongly for me versus just confirm dates
I exported my LinkedIn data and I want to turn it into an actual strategic asset instead of a vanity metric
principles: Relationships decay over time using half-life mathematics; every week without contact erodes relationship strength
Reciprocity imbalances reveal who you can ask favors from (those who owe you) vs. who you should give to first (those you owe)
Vouch likelihood is a composite signal combining message depth, recency, recommendations, endorsements, and shared tenure—not just connection status
Dormant conversations with built-in re-engagement hooks are lower-effort and higher-probability than cold outreach
Network archetype determines optimal strategy; generic advice fails because different network shapes require different approaches
For niche target companies, relevance outweighs warmth in warm-path scoring (70% weighting); for well-known companies, warmth matters more
Your data should serve your questions, not the platform's engagement metrics
steps: Export LinkedIn data archive (connections, messages, endorsements, recommendations, positions, skills, profile CSVs)
Calculate relationship half-life scores: initial strength × 0.5^(T/180), adjusted +90 days for shared company history, +60 days for deep message threads, -60 days for shallow interactions
Build reciprocity debt ledger: assign point values to given/received recommendations (5 pts) and endorsements (1 pt); compute net balance per connection to identify ask-list vs. give-first contacts

Compute vouch scores (0–100) per connection: message depth (up to 40 pts) + recency (20 pts if <6 months, 10 pts if 6–12 months) + recommendations written for you (20 pts each) + endorsements per 3 (10 pts) + shared company tenure (15 pts)
Scan message history for resurrection opportunities: flag threads with unscheduled catch-ups, unanswered help requests, unfulfilled offers, and job-change re-entry points
Classify network archetype (Thought Leader, Insider, Connector, Climber, Builder) based on inbound connection rates, company concentration, title density, and startup vs. enterprise mix

Run warm-path discovery for any target company: rank connections by combined relevance score (domain keywords, adjacent companies, investor/founder roles) × warmth score, weighted 70% relevance for niche targets

Map each analysis output to a concrete action: half-life → who to contact this week; reciprocity ledger → who to ask for favors; vouch scores → reference list qualification; resurrection list → quick-win outreach; archetype → strategy selection; warm path → introduction request

source_posts.title: Cold applications have a <2% response rate now + the warm path system that replaces them (includes a guide and prompts!)

frameworks.example_application: This network is a Connector archetype — high diversity across companies and industries, but shallow message depth with most connections. The vouch score list is thin: only 12 connections score above 60, and 8 of those are from the same former employer. The reciprocity ledger shows three people who wrote recommendations and received nothing back — those are the give-first priorities before any asks. For the target company (a Series B climate-tech startup), the warm-path scoring weights relevance at 70%: the strongest path isn't the closest friend but a second-degree connection who spent three years at a competitor and has a live message thread with a resurrection hook — an unanswered coffee offer from four months ago.

frameworks.name: Context Gap Analysis for Human-AI Complementarity
frameworks.description: A four-step diagnostic procedure for identifying where AI enforcement can address structural human cognitive limitations in any domain, and how to design the resulting human-AI handoff.
when_to_apply: The same quality standards keep slipping despite everyone agreeing they matter and knowing the rules
We're trying to decide which parts of our review or QA process to give to AI versus keep as human judgment
Quality degrades gradually across a large codebase or content surface and nobody can monitor all of it
Our best people catch things that average performers miss, and we want to scale that attention without depending on heroics
Recurring failures keep happening that aren't really about skill — the information existed, it just wasn't in the right person's head at the right moment
principles: Most quality failures are context problems, not people problems — the information needed to prevent failures exists but isn't held in mind at the moment of decision
AI has structural advantage where tasks require holding more context than humans can manage, applying rules consistently at scale, and catching deviations without fatigue
Humans retain structural advantage for novel decisions, business trade-offs, cross-system judgment, and knowing when rules should be broken
Expertise narrows the context gap but does not close it — building quality systems around heroic attention does not scale
Every enforcement system needs a designed exception mechanism, or engineers will create informal workarounds that defeat the purpose
Enforcing the wrong rules at scale is worse than not enforcing them — bad patterns in pockets may contain local wisdom that contradicts a flawed standard
steps: Step 1 — Identify your entropy: Find where things degrade despite good intentions — where agreed-upon principles don't get followed, where quality drifts over time without any single bad decision causing it. Frame this as a context problem, not a people problem.

Step 2 — Map the cognitive constraint: Determine what a person would need to hold in mind simultaneously to prevent that degradation. Ask whether a reasonable, competent person can realistically maintain that context. If the context required exceeds what any single mind can hold at decision time, you have found a structural cognitive limit.

Step 3 — Ask whether AI can address that specific limit: Determine whether the principle can be articulated as a rule, whether the AI can access the context needed to evaluate against that rule, and whether it can check consistently at scale. If yes, this is a candidate for AI enforcement. If the task requires novel judgment, business context, or understanding things that aren't written down, it remains human work.

Step 4 — Design the handoff: Define what AI handles versus what humans handle, how humans can override AI when they have context the AI lacks, and how to prevent failure modes such as deskilling, ossification, and over-standardization.

source_posts.title: My honest take on what AI is structurally better at than your best architects (and where it still falls short)

frameworks.example_application: A platform team's API designs keep violating their own published naming conventions, pagination standards, and error-response formats — not because engineers don't know the standards, but because no single person can hold 200+ existing endpoints in mind while designing a new one. That's a structural cognitive limit, not a skill gap. The rule is fully articulable ('all collection endpoints use cursor-based pagination'), the AI can access the full API surface to check against it, and it can run on every PR without fatigue. This is a clear enforcement candidate. However, the decision about whether a new endpoint should be RESTful or event-driven given the business context stays human — that requires cross-system judgment about downstream consumers that isn't written down anywhere. The handoff: AI blocks convention violations in CI with a one-click override that requires a brief rationale, preventing both drift and ossification.

frameworks.name: Agent Context Failure Catalog
frameworks.description: Nine enumerated failure modes in agent context engineering, each with a recognizable signal and root cause, enabling diagnosis of why a long-running agent breaks down.
when_to_apply: An agent performs well in short demos but fails in production tasks lasting more than 20 minutes
We upgraded to a larger context window model and performance actually got worse
Our multi-agent system keeps hallucinating despite having clear role definitions for each agent
Agent costs are scaling way faster than task complexity and we can't figure out why
We added summarization to manage context length but the agent started dropping constraints it used to follow
principles: Append-everything trap: single growing transcript causes cost scaling and attention dilution predictably around the 20–30 minute mark
Blind summarization: compressing without a schema causes constraints and failures to be silently discarded (brevity bias / context collapse)
Long-context delusion: upgrading to a larger context window without fixing accumulation makes performance worse, not better
Observability as context: debug logs and stack traces in the same buffer as task instructions drown the model in noise
Tool schema bloat: too many overlapping tools consume attention budget and create ambiguity before the agent sees any task content
Anthropomorphic multi-agent: roleplay-style agent teams sharing a giant context produce hallucination, not coordination
Static configurations: no execution feedback loop means agents never improve and re-discover every failure
Over-structured harness: elaborate routing logic prevents more capable models from using their full capabilities
Cache destruction: unstable prefixes (timestamps, non-deterministic serialization) force full-cost recomputation on identical logical content

source_posts.title: Get the Cheat Code on Long-Running AI Agents—Here's What Manus, Google, and Anthropic Learned After Trial and Error + 12 Prompts to Help Build Long-Running Agents Yourself
My honest take on what AI is structurally better at than your best architects (and where it still falls short)

frameworks.example_application: The active failure mode is the append-everything trap. The agent's task completion rate drops sharply after 25 minutes, cost per run has tripled in the last sprint, and the team's attempted fix — blind summarization — silently discarded three safety constraints from the working context, introducing a second failure mode on top of the first. The tell was that the agent 'forgot' a file-write constraint it had acknowledged fifteen minutes earlier: that's attention dilution from unbounded accumulation, compounded by lossy compression that stripped the constraint during summarization.

frameworks.name: Engineering Manager Identity Shift
frameworks.description: Reframes the AI-augmented developer's role from 'engineer who uses AI' to 'engineering manager responsible for team throughput,' changing how attention and effort are allocated.
when_to_apply: I'm using Copilot and Claude heavily but my actual shipping velocity hasn't meaningfully increased
I find myself rewriting most of what the AI produces and wondering what the point is
I'm trying to run multiple AI agents in parallel but feel cognitively overwhelmed keeping track of everything
I know AI can do more but I can't stop myself from hands-on-keyboard coding instead of delegating
The bottleneck in my workflow shifted from 'can I write this code' to 'can I coordinate all these outputs' and I don't know how to operate differently
principles: An engineering manager's job is to ensure their team produces valuable output, not to write code themselves
Agents are stateless, tireless, and prone to confident incorrectness — managing them requires different discipline than managing humans
Your value no longer lives in the code you produce; it lives in direction-setting, output review, and throughput optimization
Letting go of the 'engineer who writes elegant code' identity is leverage, not loss
Attention allocation changes fundamentally when you adopt a manager rather than contributor identity

source_posts.title: The identity shift that unlocked real throughput and how to make it stick (plus an in-depth builders guide for 2026)

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that this developer needs better prompts or a more capable model — they're reviewing every line of AI-generated code and feeling slower than before. That's wrong. The bottleneck isn't the AI's output quality; it's the developer's identity. They're still operating as an individual contributor who happens to have a tool, so they treat every AI output as their code that must meet their standards.
