The moment they reframe themselves as an engineering manager running a team of tireless but unreliable junior devs, everything shifts: attention moves from writing and polishing code to setting clear direction, triaging which outputs need deep review vs. spot-checks, and maximizing the number of parallel workstreams. The identity of 'elegant coder' was the bottleneck — not the AI.

frameworks.name: Strategic Altitude Shifting
frameworks.description: A framework for deliberately moving between high-level delegation and low-level verification when working with AI agents, avoiding the twin failure modes of permanent high-altitude vibe coding and permanent low-altitude line-by-line review.
when_to_apply: I've been vibe coding for weeks and realize I couldn't explain how my own auth system works
I'm spending hours reviewing every line of AI-generated code and my throughput has cratered
I need to debug a production issue in AI-generated code and I have no mental model of how it works
I want a practical rhythm for when to trust AI output and when to read it carefully
My codebase has grown significantly through AI generation and I need to decide which parts I actually need to understand deeply
principles: Neither staying permanently high (pure vibe coding) nor permanently low (reviewing every line) is optimal
Drop altitude deliberately at critical paths: authentication, data handling, core business logic
Verify that your mental model matches reality at key checkpoints, then climb back out
Experiential debt (gap between built and understood) is distinct from technical debt and equally costly
The skill is knowing when to change altitude, not staying at one level
steps: Delegate initial implementation to agents at high altitude
Identify critical paths where verification matters most (authentication, data handling, core logic)
Drop altitude deliberately to examine those specific areas and verify mental model against reality
Test edge cases that matter in the verified areas
Climb back out to high altitude and continue directing

source_posts.title: The identity shift that unlocked real throughput and how to make it stick (plus an in-depth builders guide for 2026)

frameworks.example_application: The authentication module and payment processing flow are critical paths — those warrant dropping altitude to read every line, trace the token flow, and verify the mental model matches what the agent actually built. The UI layout components and boilerplate CRUD endpoints are not critical paths — those stay at high altitude, accepted on trust with a quick smoke test. After verifying the auth module and confirming the session handling matches expectations, altitude climbs back up and the next three features get delegated without line-by-line review. The experiential debt is now concentrated only in non-critical areas where it's tolerable.

frameworks.name: Temporal Separation (Build/Reflect Rhythm)
frameworks.description: A cognitive architecture practice that separates the generative building state from the evaluative reflection state across different time periods to enable both high-throughput shipping and strategic improvement.
when_to_apply: I'm shipping a lot with AI but keep hitting the same problems week after week
I feel like I can't think strategically about my workflow while I'm in the middle of an active building session with agents
I want to build a feedback loop on my AI-augmented development process but don't know when or how to do the analysis
My AI-assisted work feels like plate-spinning — high throughput but no compounding improvement
I have tons of session transcripts and monitoring data but never actually review them to find patterns
principles: The generative/flow state and the evaluative/strategic state require different brain chemistry
Reflection sessions feel like overhead but are the difference between getting faster and getting better
Create artifacts during building (transcripts, monitoring data) that your future reflecting self can analyze
Strategic questions (what worked, what failed, what patterns emerged) can only be answered with temporal distance
Write drunk, edit sober — adapted for AI-augmented work
steps: During building sessions, focus on throughput — delegate, review outputs, redirect agents
Instrument your work to create reviewable artifacts (session transcripts, monitoring logs, error reports)
Schedule separate reflection sessions with temporal distance from building (e.g., build Tuesday, reflect Friday)
In reflection sessions, analyze patterns: which prompts worked, where agents got stuck, what architectural decisions are causing pain
Use reflection insights to update your approach for the next building cycle

source_posts.title: The identity shift that unlocked real throughput and how to make it stick (plus an in-depth builders guide for 2026)

frameworks.example_application: A developer has been running AI-assisted building sessions for three weeks straight, shipping features daily but noticing the same failure patterns repeating — agents hallucinating config values, prompts that need manual correction every time, architectural decisions made under time pressure that now create drag. The building sessions are high-throughput but the process never improves because there's no temporal distance for pattern recognition. Scheduling a Friday reflection session with the week's session transcripts and error logs reveals that 60% of agent failures trace to a single missing context pattern — a fix that takes 20 minutes but was invisible from inside the flow state. The next building cycle runs measurably cleaner because the reflection artifact became a rules file update.

frameworks.name: Two Kinds of Architecture
frameworks.description: Distinguishes between codifiable technical patterns (delegatable to AI agents) and 'scaling taste' — the coherence and vision quality that remains a human responsibility and cannot yet be outsourced.
when_to_apply: My AI-generated code follows all conventions perfectly but the product still feels incoherent and directionless
I'm writing an AGENTS.md file and trying to figure out what belongs in it versus what I need to keep in my own head
I'm spending my time reviewing AI-written code for style consistency when I should be doing something else — but I'm not sure what that something else is
I want to delegate more architectural decisions to agents but I'm worried about losing the coherent vision of the system
My AI-assisted project is technically sound but lacks the 'soul' that makes it feel like one person designed it
principles: Civil engineering patterns (conventions, standards, consistency) are tractable — write them down and agents can follow them
Taste, coherence, and vision ('the quality without a name') remain human work and cannot yet be delegated
Agents excel at consistent application of best practices; humans must own judgment about what feels right
Conflating these two architectures leads to misplaced expectations about what AI can produce
When dealing with civil engineering architecture, lean hard on agents; when dealing with taste, that's where your attention must go

source_posts.title: The identity shift that unlocked real throughput and how to make it stick (plus an in-depth builders guide for 2026)
Executive Briefing: What Cursor's $57K CMS Deletion Reveals About Where Agent Value Actually Lives

frameworks.example_application: The codebase is immaculate — consistent naming, proper error handling, well-structured modules — because the agent followed every convention in AGENTS.md perfectly. But the product feels like a committee designed it: five different interaction patterns for similar tasks, a settings page that implies a mental model no user actually holds, and an API surface that's technically clean but tells no coherent story. That's the tell. The civil engineering architecture is fully delegated and working. The taste architecture — the 'why does this feature exist and how does it connect to everything else' — has no owner. The builder's attention needs to shift entirely from code consistency (the agent has that) to product coherence (only they can hold that).

frameworks.name: Experiential Debt
frameworks.description: Distinguishes experiential debt (the gap between what you've built and your embodied understanding of it) from technical debt, identifying it as a separate and underappreciated risk of AI-accelerated development.
when_to_apply: I vibe-coded a working prototype but now I feel like a tourist in my own codebase
My team shipped fast with AI but our debugging time has exploded and nobody understands the architecture deeply
I'm wondering whether AI-assisted speed is actually costing me something I can't easily name
I built what I thought I wanted quickly, but now realize I never discovered what I actually needed because I skipped the messy middle
Someone on my team can demo the product but can't explain why it's built the way it is
principles: Operator's knowledge — knowing where the nooks and crannies are — cannot be built at the same speed AI builds systems
The vision for a product is often fundamentally wrong; stepwise building reveals what you actually want
Skipping intermediate phases means skipping the discoveries that reveal what you actually want to build
You can build fast and still accumulate experiential knowledge, but it requires intentionality and actually using what you ship
Experiential debt manifests as debugging time, architectural confusion, and building the wrong thing faster

source_posts.title: The identity shift that unlocked real throughput and how to make it stick (plus an in-depth builders guide for 2026)

frameworks.example_application: This team's velocity problem isn't technical debt — it's experiential debt. They used AI to scaffold an entire event-processing pipeline in two days, but nobody on the team has ever manually handled a malformed event. Now every bug takes 4x longer to diagnose because they're reverse-engineering their own system. The tell: they can describe what the system does from the README, but they can't predict what will break when inputs change. The fix isn't to slow down — it's to actually use what they shipped, run edge cases by hand, and build the operator's intuition that the AI-assisted sprint skipped over.

frameworks.name: Colleague-Shaped vs. Tool-Shaped AI Selection Framework
frameworks.description: A decision framework for choosing between iterative/collaborative AI (colleague-shaped) and autonomous/execution-focused AI (tool-shaped) based on two axes: specification clarity and verification cost.
when_to_apply: My AI agent keeps producing output that looks great but has fundamental errors I only catch later
I'm trying to decide whether to use ChatGPT-style back-and-forth or a fire-and-forget autonomous agent for a project
Junior team members are getting worse results from the same AI tools that work well for senior staff
I'm designing an AI workflow and need to decide how much human-in-the-loop interaction to build in
Someone on my team wants to switch to fully autonomous AI agents but I'm not sure they can specify tasks precisely enough
principles: The core axis is specification quality × verification cost: tool-shaped AI wins when the spec is crisp and verification is cheap; colleague-shaped AI wins when the spec is discoverable only through iteration or verification is expensive

Senior/expert practitioners benefit from tool-shaped AI because they can write precise specifications and verify outputs quickly; junior/developing practitioners benefit from colleague-shaped AI because the dialogue catches errors early and teaches simultaneously
Most people overestimate their ability to specify precise intent — the feedback loop that makes iterative AI feel slower is the same mechanism that catches errors before they compound
High-grade intent (the ability to produce complete, unambiguous specifications upfront) is a learnable skill and a prerequisite for effective use of autonomous AI
The same tool characteristic (e.g., yielding control frequently) is a bug in one context and a feature in another — context determines fit, not absolute capability
Organizations likely need both patterns simultaneously: autonomous delegation for domain experts and iterative collaboration for developing contributors

source_posts.title: The Specification Gap: Why Your AI Produces Impressive-Looking Output With Fundamental Problems + The Prompt Kit To Help You Fix It

frameworks.example_application: This team is using an autonomous coding agent but getting plausible-looking output with subtle architectural errors. The tell is specification clarity × verification cost: the junior developers can't write precise enough specs to get good autonomous output, and they lack the expertise to cheaply verify the results. They're in the colleague-shaped quadrant — iterative dialogue would catch these errors mid-stream instead of letting them compound into a finished artifact that looks right but isn't. The senior architect, by contrast, can specify exactly what she wants and spot problems in seconds — for her, the autonomous mode is correct and the iteration overhead is pure friction.

frameworks.name: Two Kinds of Disposable Software
frameworks.description: Classifies disposable software into two distinct categories with different risk profiles and strategic implications.
when_to_apply: We're adopting a 'ship fast, kill fast' approach to features and I need to figure out where that's safe versus dangerous
Someone on the team is pointing to Cursor's success with rapid iteration as a model for our enterprise product
We're using AI to generate lots of small tools and features quickly, and I need to decide which ones need reliability investment versus which can stay throwaway
Our product strategy treats AI-generated features as experiments, but customers keep complaining when we deprecate things
I'm trying to figure out whether vibe-coded tools are appropriate for internal use versus customer-facing use
principles: Personal/throwaway software (one-off dashboards, personal tools, weekend projects) is unambiguously beneficial and represents genuine democratization
Disposable features inside enterprise products carry hidden risks around trust, stability, and maintenance burden
The two categories share a name but have fundamentally different cost structures and customer tolerance levels
Simple interfaces (e.g., terminal-based) better absorb constant change than complex GUIs, making disposability more viable

source_posts.title: Disposable software works for Cursor, but probably won't work for you. + The reliability playbook for everyone else

frameworks.example_application: The team wants to ship AI-generated features rapidly and deprecate them if they don't stick — a 'disposable software' philosophy. But this is an enterprise SaaS product with paying customers, not a weekend project. That makes it Category 2: disposable features inside a product people rely on. The cost structure is completely different — customers build workflows around features, and removing them erodes trust even if usage was low. The same rapid-churn approach that's unambiguously good for personal tools and one-off dashboards becomes a liability here. A terminal-based developer tool like Cursor can absorb constant churn because its interface is simple and its users expect instability; a complex enterprise GUI with onboarding flows and integrations cannot.

frameworks.name: Code Cost vs. Attention Cost Distinction
frameworks.description: Separates the collapsed cost of generating code from the unchanged cost of directing skilled human attention toward a goal, exposing the flaw in 'software is now free' reasoning.
when_to_apply: My team says we should build it in-house because AI makes software basically free now
We're debating whether to pull engineers off the core product to vibe-code internal tools
Leadership is excited about replacing SaaS subscriptions with AI-generated internal software
Someone calculated ROI on AI-assisted development but only counted the coding time saved
We keep generating new internal tools with AI but our senior engineers are drowning in maintenance and security fixes
principles: The cost of generating code has collapsed to near zero; the cost of human attention directed at a goal has not
Opportunity cost of diverting senior builders from core mission is incalculable regardless of how cheap the software is to generate
Maintenance burden does not disappear with cheap initial generation — it shifts from upfront engineering to ongoing remediation
AI-generated code introduces security vulnerabilities that require skilled human review, adding back hidden costs
The constraint was always attention, not software cost

source_posts.title: Disposable software works for Cursor, but probably won't work for you. + The reliability playbook for everyone else

frameworks.example_application: The team wants to vibe-code an internal billing dashboard instead of paying $2K/month for a SaaS tool, arguing that Cursor makes it nearly free. That's code cost thinking. The real cost is three weeks of a senior engineer's attention — someone currently architecting the core product's payment integration. The code generation takes hours; the specification, security review, edge-case handling, and ongoing maintenance consume the same skilled attention they always did. The $2K/month SaaS is buying back the most constrained resource the company has: directed senior attention on the core mission.

frameworks.name: Developer Customers vs. CIO Customers Chasm
frameworks.description: Classifies enterprise software buyers into two archetypes with fundamentally different tolerances and expectations, determining which product philosophy is viable.
when_to_apply: We're shipping features fast and breaking things, but our enterprise customers keep escalating to their account managers
Debating whether our AI startup can displace an incumbent like ServiceNow or Workday by iterating faster
Our product team wants to adopt a disposable-software philosophy but we sell to Fortune 500 procurement teams
Trying to figure out why the same product strategy that works for developer tools is failing in our enterprise segment
Designing our support model and SLA tiers and unsure how much instability our customer base will tolerate
principles: Developer customers can fix things when they break; CIO customers call their account manager
Developers chose bleeding-edge tools knowing they would change; CIOs chose vendors with SLAs specifically to avoid thinking about the software
The gap between these customer types is not a temporary gap that closes as AI improves — it is a fundamental difference in what is being purchased
Enterprise customers are buying reliability and peace of mind, not features
CIO customers need a 'single ringable neck' — someone accountable when things fail

source_posts.title: Disposable software works for Cursor, but probably won't work for you. + The reliability playbook for everyone else

frameworks.example_application: This SaaS startup wants to ship weekly model updates and deprecate old API endpoints on a 30-day cycle, Cursor-style. But their buyers are mid-market operations teams whose CIOs selected this vendor after a six-month procurement process specifically for stability guarantees. These are CIO customers, not developer customers — they don't have engineers who can patch around breaking changes at 2am. The rapid-iteration playbook that works for developer-tool companies will generate support tickets, churn, and contract non-renewals here. The product philosophy needs to be proactive reliability with a 'single ringable neck,' not move-fast-and-ship.

frameworks.name: Proactively Reliable AI: The Two-Step Enterprise Strategy
frameworks.description: A sequential two-step framework for enterprise software companies to earn the right to deploy autonomous AI agents by first establishing reliability, then layering in proactive capability.
when_to_apply: Our enterprise customers keep asking for AI features but we still have reliability issues they complain about
We're building an AI agent that takes actions on behalf of users and need to figure out how aggressively to automate
An AI-native competitor is winning developer mindshare but we have the enterprise trust — how do we sequence our AI roadmap?
Product leadership wants to ship proactive AI capabilities but our NPS scores show customers don't fully trust the platform yet
We're debating whether our AI should suggest actions or take them autonomously for enterprise customers
principles: Reliability is table stakes — without it, proactive AI creates anxiety rather than value
You cannot skip step one: attempting proactivity before proving reliability will terrify customers
Reactive AI (chatbots) waits to be asked and is no longer a differentiator; proactive AI creates value customers didn't know they were missing
Trust is earned incrementally — start with low-stakes autonomous actions and build a track record of correct decisions
Earned trust is the precondition for autonomous action on behalf of users
steps: Step 1 — Establish reliability: Prove your product works consistently, data is secure, SLAs are met, and customers have a human to call when something goes wrong. This must come before any autonomous AI capability.

Step 2 — Layer in proactive AI: Once reliability is proven and trust is earned, deploy agents that take autonomous action on behalf of users without being asked — surfacing insights, updating records, drafting responses, alerting stakeholders — creating value customers didn't know they were missing.

source_posts.title: Disposable software works for Cursor, but probably won't work for you. + The reliability playbook for everyone else

frameworks.example_application: The product team wants to ship an AI agent that auto-reassigns support tickets based on urgency signals. But customers still file escalations about data sync delays twice a month, and there's no dedicated support line — just a chatbot. Deploying autonomous reassignment now will feel like the system is making decisions customers can't trust or override. The right move is to close the reliability gap first: hit the SLA consistently, give customers a human escalation path, then earn the right to auto-reassign by starting with low-stakes suggestions ('we would have reassigned this — approve?') before graduating to full autonomy.

frameworks.name: Tool vs. Infrastructure Design Question
frameworks.description: Challenges builders to decide whether they are creating a standalone tool that solves one problem or infrastructure that other systems can build on top of, because the choice determines design decisions and long-term leverage.
when_to_apply: I'm building a personal productivity system and wondering whether to add an API or keep it simple
I keep rebuilding the same components across different projects and wondering if I should create a shared foundation
Deciding whether my Notion/Obsidian setup should just work for me or serve as a hub that other automations connect to
I built a workflow that works great for one use case but now I want three other things to use its data
Trying to figure out how much modularity and extensibility to invest in upfront versus shipping something that just works
principles: A tool solves a problem; infrastructure enables other things to be built on top of it
Designing with infrastructure in mind creates leverage: one investment pays dividends across everything that connects to it
Infrastructure thinking changes data model choices, API exposure decisions, and how modular components are built
The same architectural patterns scale from simple personal tools to sophisticated multi-system infrastructure without breaking

source_posts.title: 50 people ignored my tool recommendations + here's why their systems still worked (Second Brain follow-up)

frameworks.example_application: This note-taking system is being designed as a tool — it captures and retrieves notes, full stop. But the user wants their task manager, writing workflow, and AI agents to all pull from the same data. That's infrastructure, not a tool. The data model needs to change: structured fields instead of free-text blobs, stable IDs that external systems can reference, and an API layer even if the only consumer today is one Zapier integration. The tell was 'I want my other systems to build on this' — that sentence means infrastructure, and the current flat-file design will break the moment a second system tries to consume it.

frameworks.name: The Bidirectional Fit Assessment Interface
frameworks.description: Reframes job-seeking from one-directional credential presentation to a mutual fit assessment where the candidate's interface actively evaluates and can reject mismatched opportunities.
when_to_apply: I have deep expertise but keep getting rejected at the resume screen by people who can't evaluate what I actually do
I want to build a professional presence that works asynchronously — something that represents me when I'm not in the room
How do I stand out in a job market flooded with AI-polished resumes that all sound the same?
I'm tired of dumbing down my experience to fit a one-page resume format
I want employers to feel like they discovered my strengths rather than being pitched at
principles: Replace credential assertion with capability demonstration — an interactive interface that can be interrogated is harder to fake than a polished document
Make the fit assessment bidirectional — the tool should honestly tell employers when you are NOT a good match, not just pitch your strengths
Depth of response signals real expertise — multi-turn AI conversations about your work only hold up if genuine understanding underlies them
Publishing your gaps builds more trust than claiming universal competence
Honest rejection of bad fits signals market confidence and saves both parties time
The interface functions as proof of capability, not a claim of capability — evaluators feel they discovered the truth rather than being told it
The work required to build the interface (articulating expertise, identifying genuine strengths and gaps) improves the underlying substance it represents
steps: Choose one interface element to build first (AI-queryable summary, expanded achievement context, or fit assessment tool)
Write a dense structured document of your real work organized for AI parsing, not human scanning — include specific projects, numbers, lessons, and honest gaps

Write a system prompt governing how AI represents you: be specific, cite actual work, acknowledge limitations honestly, include explicit anti-sycophancy instructions and permission to reject mismatched roles
Build the simplest viable version (structured document + instructions for use, Custom GPT, or web interface depending on available time)
Publish it somewhere visible and distribute it through existing channels
Refine based on observed queries — add context where AI responses lack depth, cut material that never gets queried, improve prompts based on edge cases

source_posts.title: Why it's time to escape the application pile + the exact site I shipped (no code required!)

frameworks.example_application: A senior data engineer with 8 years of experience keeps getting filtered out by keyword-matching ATS systems because their resume compresses deep pipeline architecture work into generic bullet points. The conventional approach is to optimize the resume for more keywords. That's wrong here — optimization for keyword density compresses expertise further and makes them indistinguishable from junior candidates who've memorized the same terms. Instead, they build a queryable interface: a structured document of their actual projects (with real metrics, architectural decisions, and honest gaps like 'limited Spark Streaming experience') paired with a Custom GPT that can answer multi-turn technical questions about their work. When a hiring manager asks 'How did you handle schema evolution across 40 microservices?', the interface gives a detailed, cite-specific answer that no resume padding could survive. The interface also explicitly flags mismatches — 'This candidate has no production ML pipeline experience; if that's core to the role, this isn't a fit' — which paradoxically increases trust in every positive claim it makes.

frameworks.name: Asserting Credentials vs. Demonstrating Capability
frameworks.description: Distinguishes between telling evaluators what to believe about you (resume assertions) versus creating conditions for evaluators to discover your capability through their own exploration of an interactive interface.
when_to_apply: My resume looks the same as everyone else's because AI can generate polished bullets for anyone
I have deep expertise but evaluators keep treating me like every other applicant with similar-sounding credentials
I'm deciding whether to build a traditional portfolio or something interactive that lets people explore my work
Hiring managers in my field have become skeptical of polished application materials because they assume AI wrote everything
I want to stand out in a job search but I'm worried that more polish just looks like better prompting
principles: People believe conclusions they reach themselves more than conclusions they are told — design for discovery, not declaration
AI-mediated self-presentation makes depth almost impossible to fake because multi-turn interrogation surfaces what is actually there
Polish in a document proves only access to AI tools; depth in an interactive interface proves genuine understanding
Honest acknowledgment of gaps in an interface demonstrates self-awareness, which itself is a credibility signal
You architect the discovery conditions; the evaluator feels they formed their own judgment

source_posts.title: Why it's time to escape the application pile + the exact site I shipped (no code required!)

frameworks.example_application: This candidate's portfolio site is a static PDF with impressive bullet points — that's asserting credentials, not demonstrating capability. In a world where Claude can produce those same bullets for anyone, the signal value is zero. The candidate who built an interactive interface where the evaluator can ask follow-up questions, drill into edge cases, and probe reasoning depth is on the other side of the distinction — the evaluator discovers the expertise themselves and trusts it precisely because they feel they formed their own judgment rather than being told what to believe.

frameworks.name: The Bottleneck Relocation Model
frameworks.description: Reframes workplace chaos and inefficiency as a predictable consequence of the bottleneck moving from execution to four new scarce resources (clarity, ambition, distribution, relationships), and diagnoses which old habits were built to protect the wrong constraint.
when_to_apply: Our team adopted AI tools and got faster at building, but somehow our output quality and impact went down
We have all these planning ceremonies and approval gates that used to feel essential but now feel like bureaucratic theater
I can build anything in a weekend now but I'm paralyzed about what to build — the hard part completely flipped
We're trying to figure out which organizational processes to kill versus keep after a major capability upgrade
My old workflow was optimized for a world where building was expensive, and it's not working anymore but I can't articulate why
principles: Every work system is implicitly organized around protecting whatever resource is most scarce
When a bottleneck is eliminated, it relocates downstream rather than disappearing
When execution gets cheap, the new scarce resources become clarity, ambition, distribution, and relationships
Habits and rituals designed to protect the old bottleneck become waste once the bottleneck moves
Judgment, taste, and knowing what's worth building become more valuable as the cost of building falls

source_posts.title: Grab the prompt kit I use when work feels inefficient but busy + specific experiments for each bottleneck

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that the team needs better project management because they're shipping lots of mediocre work. That's wrong here — the bottleneck relocated. Execution used to be scarce, so every ritual (sprint planning, PRDs, approval gates) was designed to protect execution capacity from waste. Now execution is cheap — AI handles most of the building — but the team never reorganized around what's actually scarce: clarity about what's worth building and distribution to get it in front of the right people. The sprint ceremonies aren't enabling work anymore; they're protecting a constraint that no longer exists, which means they're pure drag. The investment should shift to taste-setting rituals (what's worth building?) and distribution habits (who sees it and why?).

frameworks.name: Old-Ritual Failure Catalog
frameworks.description: Enumerates eight specific work habits that were rational under expensive-execution economics but now waste time or hide judgment, each with its original logic, its failure mode in the new environment, and a concrete substitute behavior.
when_to_apply: My team is busy all the time but our actual output velocity feels embarrassingly low
We have powerful AI tools available but our process still feels like it did two years ago
Someone on the team is spending more time preparing to do the work than actually doing it
I keep waiting for approvals or alignment meetings before I can make progress on something low-risk
Our workflow has a lot of steps that feel like they exist to manage risk but the risk they manage is tiny compared to the delay they cause
principles: Permission loops distribute accountability but cost more time than the risk they hedge when execution is cheap
Polish can be a form of procrastination and ego protection masquerading as diligence
Meetings surface opinions but rarely resolve questions as cleanly as a prototype does
Waiting for approvals or decisions now costs more than making provisional decisions and correcting course
Planning elaborates assumptions without generating learning; learning only happens when something is built
A deck describes a thing; a demo is the thing—the former invites abstract argument, the latter anchors discussion in reality
Consensus before action costs more than acting and reporting results, because people align around data more than proposals
Hoarding work until it feels ready delays feedback to the point where changing course is expensive

source_posts.title: Grab the prompt kit I use when work feels inefficient but busy + specific experiments for each bottleneck

frameworks.example_application: The team spent three days building a slide deck to get leadership alignment on a feature direction. That's the 'deck instead of demo' failure mode — the original logic was that building was expensive so you had to secure buy-in before committing resources, but now a working prototype takes less time than the deck does. The deck invited two rounds of abstract debate about hypotheticals that a clickable demo would have resolved in the first meeting. The substitute: build the simplest version, show it, let people react to reality instead of a description of reality.

frameworks.name: AI Usage vs. AI Leverage Distinction
frameworks.description: Separates the act of using AI tools (activity) from actually achieving different, measurable outputs through AI (leverage), preventing workers and organizations from confusing adoption metrics with genuine capability improvement.
when_to_apply: My team all uses AI tools now but I can't point to any measurable improvement in our output
We're tracking how often employees use ChatGPT or Copilot and I'm not sure that metric tells us anything real
Someone on my team talks a lot about AI but their actual deliverables look the same as before
Our company mandated AI adoption and everyone complied, but nothing seems to have actually changed
I want to distinguish between employees who are genuinely transformed by AI and those who are just performing adoption
principles: 'I use AI' is an activity claim; 'my output is different now' is a leverage claim — only the latter has value
Performative productivity emerges when usage is measured instead of outcomes
AI leverage requires workflow restructuring, not just tool insertion into existing processes
The gap between usage and leverage is what separates companies with compounding AI advantage from those with the appearance of transformation

source_posts.title: Shopify's AI Memo Was a Filter, Not a Productivity Play. Grab the AI Leverage Audit I built after watching Duolingo fail and Shopify succeed.

frameworks.example_application: This team reports 92% AI adoption — every member uses Copilot daily — but their sprint velocity, code quality metrics, and feature throughput are statistically identical to six months ago. That's usage, not leverage. The tell: they inserted AI into existing workflows without restructuring any of them. The developer who actually has leverage is the one who eliminated the entire manual QA review step by building an AI-driven test generation pipeline — her output is structurally different, not just AI-assisted.

frameworks.name: Two AI Economies Framework
frameworks.description: A classification system that sorts work into two distinct AI economies—abundance/production and judgment/complexity—each with a matched tool philosophy and risk posture.
when_to_apply: I'm trying to figure out whether it's okay to trust AI output without heavy review for this particular task
My team uses the same review process for every AI-assisted deliverable and it feels wrong — some things we over-check and others we under-check
I'm building a career strategy around AI and need to understand where human expertise still commands a premium versus where speed wins
We're debating whether to adopt AI aggressively across the board or take a cautious approach, and neither extreme feels right
I need to set different AI risk tolerances for different parts of our workflow but don't have a clear framework for which is which
principles: Tasks that produce outputs (content, drafts, media, creative exploration) belong to the production/abundance economy where speed and volume matter most
Tasks that exercise judgment (production code, legal analysis, medical decisions, high-stakes analysis) belong to the complexity/judgment economy where reliability and verifiability matter most
In the production economy, adopt aggressively—competitors will, and the market handles benefits automatically
In the judgment economy, prioritize adoption quality over adoption speed—preserve human judgment alongside AI assistance
The advantage in the production economy is knowing what to do with outputs, not just having the tools
The advantage in the judgment economy is the human expertise the AI amplifies, not the AI itself
Using the same risk posture for all tasks is the primary failure mode—generating freely when you should verify, or over-reviewing when speed matters

source_posts.title: Two founders, two safety theories, two products—and a framework for knowing which one matches your risk tolerance

frameworks.example_application: Writing marketing copy for A/B testing falls squarely in the production/abundance economy — errors are cheap, iteration is fast, and the competitive advantage goes to whoever generates and tests more variants. The team should use the fastest, most aggressive AI tools available and stop over-reviewing drafts. But the same team's contract review workflow belongs to the judgment/complexity economy: an undetected clause error creates real liability. There, the advantage comes from the lawyer's expertise being amplified by AI, not replaced by it, and adoption quality matters far more than adoption speed. The failure happening right now is that legal is reviewing AI-generated contracts with the same casual posture the marketing team rightly uses for ad copy.

frameworks.name: AI as Multiplier (The Multiplier Insight)
frameworks.description: Reframes AI leverage not as a function of prompts or tools but as a function of the depth of context and expertise being multiplied, making knowledge infrastructure the primary investment.
when_to_apply: I've tried multiple AI tools and workflows but my output quality hasn't meaningfully improved
Prioritizing between building domain knowledge vs. learning more AI techniques
Explaining to a team why two people using the same AI tools get wildly different results
Deciding whether to invest time in prompt engineering courses or in systematizing my professional knowledge
I feel like I'm getting faster but not smarter with AI
principles: AI is a multiplier, so its value is determined by what it multiplies, not by the multiplier itself
Shallow context multiplied produces faster shallow output; deep expertise multiplied produces qualitatively different output
The strategic question is 'what am I multiplying?' not 'which tools should I use?'
Building compounding context (captured knowledge, relationships, project history) is the highest-leverage AI investment
Infrastructure that lets AI amplify accumulated expertise outperforms any prompt optimization

source_posts.title: Why every system you've tried has failed + grab the 90-minute guide to one that won't

frameworks.example_application: Two consultants use the same Claude setup with similar prompts. One produces boilerplate strategy decks; the other produces insights clients call transformative. The difference isn't prompt skill — it's that the second consultant has 15 years of encoded pattern recognition, a personal knowledge base of 200+ engagements, and documented frameworks from every failure. AI is multiplying deep, structured expertise in one case and multiplying surface-level familiarity in the other. The highest-leverage move for the first consultant isn't a better prompt template — it's spending six months building the knowledge infrastructure that gives AI something worth amplifying.

frameworks.name: The Factory Curve
frameworks.description: Reframes AI competition from model capability to supply chain position, arguing that the binding constraint has shifted from research milestones to physical factory economics (memory allocation, packaging capacity, power).
when_to_apply: Is the current AI infrastructure buildout a bubble, or is demand genuinely outrunning physical supply?
We're debating whether to lock in GPU/memory capacity now or wait for prices to drop — what's the real risk of waiting?
Our AI product roadmap assumes compute availability that our vendor hasn't actually guaranteed
Why is our competitor shipping faster when our model is technically better?
Trying to understand which companies in the AI stack have real structural advantages versus hype-driven valuations
principles: Bubbles don't pre-buy bottlenecks — upstream procurement behavior (wafer-level memory, packaging slots, power agreements) reveals whether demand is real
Supply ramps slowly due to physics and permitting; capital alone cannot accelerate it
Demand compounds with state — stateful/agentic workloads grow memory footprint faster than request count
'Catch up later' doesn't work — falling behind the curve means paying spot prices or queuing, not gradually closing the gap
The unit of competition is the integrated system (factory module), not the individual component or model

source_posts.title: Why CES 2026 marks a turning point + the constraint map behind the headlines (and yes, there are prompts)

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that Company A is behind because its benchmark scores trail the frontier by six months. That's wrong here. Company A pre-bought 18 months of HBM packaging capacity and locked 200MW of power in three regions. Company B has a better model on paper but is already queuing inference jobs and paying spot rates for memory allocation. The binding constraint isn't the model — it's the factory curve. Company A can serve stateful agentic workloads at scale next quarter; Company B cannot, regardless of research velocity. The tell that this isn't a bubble: upstream suppliers are reporting committed wafer-level memory purchases with 18-month lead times, not speculative option contracts.

frameworks.name: Four-Lane Supply Strategy
frameworks.description: A classification of four distinct supply chain lanes that map to different factory bottlenecks, used to evaluate whether an AI infrastructure strategy addresses all binding constraints.
when_to_apply: We've secured GPU capacity but I'm worried we're missing other infrastructure bottlenecks that will surface in 12-18 months
Evaluating whether a competitor's AI infrastructure position is actually durable or just addresses the most visible constraint
Building a multi-vendor AI supply chain and need to identify which lanes we haven't covered
Our custom silicon program is on track but I'm not sure we've thought about upstream physical inputs like memory
Stress-testing an AI infrastructure procurement plan to find gaps before they become crises
principles: Each lane solves a distinct constraint — time, supply risk, unit economics, and physical input scarcity
A complete strategy requires coverage across all four lanes, not just the most visible one
Multi-vendor sourcing across lanes mirrors multi-cloud logic — diversification reduces chokepoint risk
Lane 4 (upstream physical inputs like memory at wafer level) is the most binding and hardest to acquire late
steps: Lane 1 — Bridge capacity: Solve the time constraint by securing rental-at-scale access while longer-term infrastructure comes online
Lane 2 — Second-source compute: Solve supply risk by establishing a second GPU ecosystem or specialized infrastructure outside primary vendors
Lane 3 — Custom silicon: Solve unit economics by pursuing purpose-built accelerators for predictable high-volume inference workloads
Lane 4 — Memory supply: Solve the binding physical constraint by engaging memory suppliers at the wafer level as a strategic input

source_posts.title: Why CES 2026 marks a turning point + the constraint map behind the headlines (and yes, there are prompts)

frameworks.example_application: This company has locked in massive GPU reservations with a hyperscaler (Lane 1 bridge capacity) and started a custom silicon program (Lane 3), but has zero second-source compute relationship outside NVIDIA (Lane 2 gap) and no direct engagement with HBM suppliers at the wafer level (Lane 4 gap). The custom silicon bet won't matter if they can't secure memory allocation — Lane 4 is the binding constraint, and by the time they realize it, wafer commitments will already be locked up by competitors who moved 18 months earlier. Two of four lanes are uncovered, which means this infrastructure position is structurally fragile despite looking impressive on the compute side.

frameworks.name: Ambient Failure Cascade
frameworks.description: Enumerates how ambient (always-on) AI systems produce categorically different failure modes than request-based AI, following a predictable cascade from degradation through liability to system pullback.
when_to_apply: We're moving from a request-based AI feature to an always-on ambient system and need to understand what new failure modes we're accepting
Our AI vendor's SLA covers uptime but I'm worried about silent quality degradation that nobody would catch
We had an incident where the AI system didn't flag something it should have — how do we think about the full downstream exposure?
Leadership wants to treat our continuous inference system with the same governance model we use for our chatbot
We're designing reliability and governance requirements for an AI system that runs without per-request human review
principles: Degradation → missed signal → harm → investigation → liability → pullback is the standard cascade sequence
The critical failure mode shifts from 'bad answer' to 'not there when needed'
Reliability becomes existential — failure modes tolerable in occasional-use systems become unacceptable in always-on systems
Governance becomes operational — compliance must be explainable in real time at scale, not checked at deployment
Downtime becomes political when people depend on inference being continuously available
SLAs covering uptime do not cover inference quality degradation — these are distinct failure surfaces

source_posts.title: Why CES 2026 marks a turning point + the constraint map behind the headlines (and yes, there are prompts)

frameworks.example_application: The ambient monitoring system didn't crash — it quietly degraded inference quality over three weeks, missing a pattern it would have flagged at full fidelity. The missed signal led to a patient safety incident, which triggered a regulatory investigation. The vendor's SLA covered uptime (99.9%) but said nothing about inference quality, so the liability landed entirely on the deploying organization. This is the standard cascade: degradation → missed signal → harm → investigation → liability → pullback. The failure mode was never 'bad answer' — it was 'not there when needed,' which is categorically harder to detect and categorically more dangerous.

frameworks.name: Constraints vs. Preferences vs. Proof vs. Confidence Distinction
frameworks.description: A four-part vocabulary for classifying work requirements so that teams can separate machine-checkable gates from human-judgment calls, enabling reliable agent delegation.
when_to_apply: My agent loop keeps running in circles and never seems to converge on a final output
I'm writing acceptance criteria for a task I want to delegate to an AI agent and I'm not sure what counts as 'done'
Some of my quality standards are gut-feel things like 'professional tone' and I need to figure out which checks to automate vs. review myself
I can't tell whether the agent actually verified something or just expressed confidence that it's correct
I want to build an automated review layer but I'm struggling to formalize what 'good' looks like for every dimension
principles: Constraints are what must be true and are objectively checkable ('must include a recommendation', 'must not exceed one page')
Preferences are what you'd like but cannot be verified by a system ('should feel professional', 'should be compelling') — these require human evaluation
Proof is a checkable artifact: the source link exists, the number reconciles, the quote appears in the transcript
Confidence is a belief state ('I think this is correct') — it cannot be verified by a loop and requires human review at that stage
Repeatable standards (always true regardless of context) can be built into automated checks; situational standards (meaning varies by context) require human judgment each time
If you cannot convert a preference into a constraint, you must evaluate it yourself — it cannot be delegated to a loop

source_posts.title: My honest field notes on the verification gap no one's talking about, plus the complete guide + prompt kit that makes agent loops actually converge

frameworks.example_application: The brief says the output 'must include three sourced recommendations' and 'should feel strategic.' The first requirement is a constraint — an agent loop can check whether exactly three recommendations exist and whether each has a source link (proof). The second is a preference — 'feels strategic' is a belief about tone that no automated check can verify. The team was stuck because their eval loop kept rejecting drafts on vibes it couldn't measure. Splitting the spec into checkable constraints and human-reviewed preferences means the loop converges on structure while a human makes the final taste call on tone.

frameworks.name: Problem Portfolio Assessment
frameworks.description: A four-question diagnostic applied to each problem you are paid to solve that classifies whether each skill is appreciating or depreciating in value, surfacing where to invest versus exit.
when_to_apply: I have a nagging sense that half of what I do every day could be done by AI in a year, but I'm not sure which half
I'm preparing for a career conversation and need to articulate my value beyond my job title or tech stack
I want to figure out which parts of my role to actively grow versus which to hand off or automate away
I'm considering a career pivot and need to know which of my capabilities are portable versus locked to my current employer
My performance review is coming up and I realize I can't clearly name the three problems that justify my compensation
principles: Define your portfolio by the three to five problems that would go unsolved if you disappeared — not your title or skill list
Scarcity of substitutes determines value: the shorter the list of people who can solve a problem without supervision, the more valuable it is
Consequence severity matters: high-downside problems command premium value for the skill to solve them correctly
Assess AI directionality per problem: some problems are being automated (depreciating), others become more judgment-intensive as output volume increases (appreciating)
Transferability multiplies value: skill that travels across companies and contexts is worth more than knowledge locked to one context
steps: List the three to five problems you are actually paid to solve — stated as what would go unsolved, not as job functions
For each problem, answer: How many others could solve this without supervision?
For each problem, answer: What breaks if it is solved poorly — money, trust, speed, or safety?
For each problem, answer: Does AI make this cheaper to do, or does it make mistakes more expensive to catch?
For each problem, answer: Does this skill transfer across companies and contexts, or is it locked to your current situation?
Classify each problem as appreciating, depreciating, or neutral based on the four answers
Identify the gap between where you spend time and where the appreciating problems sit

source_posts.title: My honest field notes on being my own unreliable narrator + the governance mechanism I finally built to help

frameworks.example_application: A senior data engineer defines their real portfolio as: (1) designing data pipelines for novel integrations, (2) debugging production data quality incidents under time pressure, (3) writing migration scripts, (4) mentoring junior engineers, (5) vendor evaluation for data tools. Problem 3 — migration scripts — has few substitutes today but AI is rapidly closing that gap; it's depreciating. Problem 2 — debugging production incidents where wrong data could cascade into billing errors — has high consequence severity, few people who can do it unsupervised, and AI actually makes it harder because automated pipelines create more failure surface area; it's appreciating. The gap is clear: 40% of weekly time goes to migration scripts, less than 10% to building systematic incident diagnosis capability. The reallocation target writes itself.

frameworks.name: Magnifying-Glass Company vs. Tiger-Team Company
frameworks.description: A strategic fork distinguishing organizations that use AI primarily for visibility and oversight from those that use AI to multiply execution power in small, high-trust teams.
when_to_apply: We're rolling out AI productivity scoring and our best people seem disengaged — is the tool the problem?
Our dashboards show improving metrics but actual product velocity feels slower than before we added all this visibility tooling
I'm deciding whether to invest our AI budget in management oversight tools or in giving small teams better execution capabilities
High-performing teams that used to operate autonomously are now spending significant time on reporting and legibility work
We have extensive AI-powered metrics but I suspect people are gaming the measurements rather than doing better work
principles: Legibility should follow work, not dictate it — AI should reconstruct what happened after the fact, not impose structure before
The magnifying-glass path selects for the feeling of control; the tiger-team path selects for the reality of output
Surveillance creates concealment: when measurement systems reward clean legibility, real messy work goes underground
When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure — AI accelerates this failure mode by making the measurement layer cheap and authoritative-looking
Small, high-trust teams with clear scope and autonomy are the primary production units of value
AI's role in a tiger-team company is as translator and historian, not bureaucrat or overseer

source_posts.title: Grab the 4 prompts I use to make messy work legible--without killing what made it valuable + the visibility trap most companies fall into (and how to avoid it)

frameworks.example_application: This organization is a magnifying-glass company. The tell: they just deployed AI-powered productivity dashboards across engineering, and their best engineers are now spending 30% of their time making work legible to the dashboard rather than doing the work. Sprint velocity looks great on the executive deck, but the three senior engineers who drove 60% of the team's real output are interviewing elsewhere. Meanwhile, the messy experimental work that produced last quarter's breakthrough feature has stopped entirely — nobody will touch ambiguous projects that score poorly on the visibility tools. The AI investment is selecting for the feeling of control while destroying the conditions that produce output.

frameworks.name: Legible vs. Illegible Work
frameworks.description: A classification that separates work that fits neatly into organizational systems (tickets, OKRs, dashboards) from the informal, trust-based, backchannel work that actually keeps companies running.
when_to_apply: Our top performer's contributions don't show up in any dashboard or OKR, and I'm worried they'll get passed over or managed out
We're rolling out AI productivity monitoring and I need to think about what it will actually capture versus what it will miss
During a crisis, the people who stepped up weren't the ones on the org chart — how do I protect that dynamic without formalizing it to death?
We're deciding which informal processes to formalize and I'm worried about killing the fast paths that actually keep us running
A team looks great on paper metrics but something feels off about their actual output and impact
principles: Illegible work — favors, backchannels, shared intuition, emergency response — is the actual engine of value, not a supplement to legible work
The legible layer is scaffolding: necessary and useful, but not where value gets created
The company tells the truth about itself in emergencies: who people actually go to reveals the real org chart
AI amplifies illegible work by giving small teams leverage, making the illegible layer more powerful and more at risk from surveillance
Tiger teams — ad hoc small groups that form organically to handle crises — are the clearest expression of illegible work in action

source_posts.title: Grab the 4 prompts I use to make messy work legible--without killing what made it valuable + the visibility trap most companies fall into (and how to avoid it)

frameworks.example_application: This team's dashboards show green across every OKR, but the product launch nearly failed until three people outside the formal project structure stepped in to unblock vendor negotiations and rewrite the integration spec over a weekend. That rescue operation — the tiger team that formed organically around the crisis — is the illegible layer doing the real work. The legible metrics can't see it, which means the next reorg might eliminate the exact people who saved the launch. The performance system is measuring scaffolding and calling it the building.

frameworks.name: The Potemkin Organization Diagnostic
frameworks.description: A structured check for whether AI-generated dashboards and reports are producing genuine organizational understanding or a confident-looking map that has drifted from reality.
when_to_apply: Our AI dashboards all show green but something still feels off — teams are struggling and customers are unhappy despite the metrics
I suspect my team is writing status updates to trigger the right signals in our AI reporting tool rather than describing what's actually happening
We deployed an AI-powered management visibility layer and I want to check whether it's actually improving decisions or just generating confident noise
An IC is pushing back on our metrics saying they don't capture what their work actually produces, and I'm not sure they're wrong
Leadership is making decisions based on AI-generated reports and I need to audit whether those reports reflect reality or a Potemkin version of it
principles: Confidence and accuracy are not the same thing — authoritative-looking outputs can be precisely wrong
Ask what a metric actually measures, then trace whether that maps to an outcome anyone cares about
Check whether teams have learned to game the inputs — writing updates to trigger desired signals rather than report reality
The danger is not blindness but overconfidence in the wrong map: a detailed, precise map that has drifted from the territory
AI drops the cost of generating the appearance of understanding toward zero, making fake visibility cheaper and more dangerous than ever
steps: Identify a dashboard, metric, or AI-generated report that feels authoritative
Ask what the metric literally measures — not what it claims to measure, but the actual data inputs
Trace whether that literal measurement maps to the outcome leadership actually cares about
Check whether teams know how the system scores them and have changed behavior to hit those scores
Determine whether the report is helping leadership understand reality or generating a confident map the organization is bending itself toward

source_posts.title: Grab the 4 prompts I use to make messy work legible--without killing what made it valuable + the visibility trap most companies fall into (and how to avoid it)

frameworks.example_application: The AI-generated sprint health dashboard shows 94% on-time delivery and green across all teams — but the metric literally measures 'stories marked done by sprint end.' Teams learned this six months ago and started splitting work into trivially small stories and marking them complete with known defects. Leadership sees a picture of execution excellence; the actual product ships late every quarter. The dashboard isn't producing understanding — it's producing the appearance of understanding, and the organization is contorting itself to feed the appearance rather than fix the reality.

frameworks.name: The Weekend-Hack Test
frameworks.description: A single-question test for whether an organization's measurement and planning systems are selecting for legibility or for value, by asking whether unplanned, off-roadmap work could survive and be recognized.
when_to_apply: We're implementing AI-powered productivity metrics and I'm worried they'll punish our best people
Our sprint process feels airtight but our best engineers say the most important work happens despite the process, not because of it
I want a quick gut-check on whether our OKR and planning system is crowding out emergent innovation
We're designing a performance review process and need to make sure it doesn't optimize for visibility over actual impact
Someone on my team just built something amazing that wasn't on any roadmap and I'm not sure our systems can even recognize it
principles: Ask: if an engineer showed up Monday with something built over the weekend — no ticket, no sprint, no OKR — would our systems flag it as a problem or recognize it as value?
The magnifying-glass company measures unplanned work out of existence; the tiger-team company protects the conditions that made it possible
The most valuable work is often the work that cannot be planned in advance because it solves problems the process cannot acknowledge
A leader's job when unplanned valuable work surfaces is not to squish it but to recognize its alignment and pull it in without killing the conditions that produced it

source_posts.title: Grab the 4 prompts I use to make messy work legible--without killing what made it valuable + the visibility trap most companies fall into (and how to avoid it)

frameworks.example_application: Last quarter, an engineer built a migration tool over a weekend that eliminated a recurring production incident — no ticket, no OKR, no sprint story. The sprint review flagged it as unplanned work, the velocity chart treated it as noise, and the performance review couldn't account for it because it didn't map to any committed objective. That's the diagnostic verdict: this organization's measurement stack is selecting for legibility over value. The most impactful work of the quarter was structurally invisible to every system that decides what counts.

frameworks.name: Three Failure Patterns of Agent Intent Misalignment
frameworks.description: Classifies the three primary ways AI agents misread user intent into distinct failure modes, each with characteristic signals and corresponding fixes.
when_to_apply: My AI agent completed a task correctly by one measure but the result feels obviously wrong in a way I can't articulate
An agent picked a valid interpretation of my request but it wasn't the one I meant, and I need to understand why
I'm doing a post-mortem on an agent action that caused real-world damage and need to classify the root cause
My agentic workflow keeps producing subtle failures and I want to know if they share a common pattern
An AI assistant did something socially inappropriate that any human colleague would have known to avoid
principles: Most agent failures fall into one of three predictable buckets, not random edge cases
Ambiguity failures occur when a model silently picks one of multiple valid interpretations without surfacing the choice
Wrong-optimization failures occur when the model improves a measurable proxy while degrading the real outcome
Social boundary failures occur when implicit human context (relationships, timing, exclusions) is missing from the instruction
The common root cause across all three is the model committing before the misread can be caught

source_posts.title: Why capable AI is a liability when intent is off + my template that makes interpretation visible before action

frameworks.example_application: The agent scheduled a client dinner and invited the founder's ex-cofounder — technically a 'key stakeholder' per the CRM data, but anyone with organizational context would know that relationship is toxic. This is a social boundary failure, not an ambiguity or optimization problem. The instruction 'invite key stakeholders' was unambiguous and the optimization target was correct — the failure is that implicit human context (who should be excluded, why, and the relational history) was never part of the agent's information set. The fix isn't better prompting; it's adding an exclusion layer or requiring human confirmation on attendee lists where relationship dynamics matter.

frameworks.name: Builder-Engineer Composability Diagnostic
frameworks.description: A set of structured questions for builders and engineers to assess their readiness for the composability era — revealing gaps in prototyping capability for builders and systemic composability gaps for engineers.
when_to_apply: Our designers and PMs keep filing tickets for things they could probably prototype themselves if they had the right skills — are they actually blocked or just not trying?
We're about to let AI generate parts of our front end and I need to know if our architecture can handle that safely
Our engineering team is 100% implementation and 0% platform/composability — is that a problem?
I want to understand whether our product team and engineering team are actually ready to collaborate differently in a world of AI-assisted UI generation
We're restructuring our front-end team and need to figure out who should be building what
principles: Builders should be able to show a working prototype, not just describe a feature — inability to do so signals a collaboration gap
Engineers should be able to articulate in one page what can vary, what cannot, and where AI can and cannot touch the UI
A composability ratio of all implementation engineers and zero composability engineers signals staffing for a prior era
The correct answer to 'what can your system generate safely' is specific and bounded — not 'nothing' or 'everything'
steps: For builders: Ask when you last built something (not specced or described it — actually built it)
For builders: Ask whether you could show your next feature idea rather than describe it
For builders: Ask whether you understand why your last three engineering requests were scoped the way they were
For engineers: Count the ratio of implementation engineers to composability engineers
For engineers: Ask what your system can generate safely and whether the answer is specific
For engineers: Ask whether you can articulate your UI generation constraints — what can vary, what can't, where AI can touch — in one page

source_posts.title: The Composability Era: What Happens When Anyone Can Build a UI (+ 4 Prompts to navigate the front-end revolution)

frameworks.example_application: The product team has five builders and twelve engineers, but zero engineers focused on composability infrastructure — the entire engineering team is writing implementation code. When asked 'what can your system generate safely?', the tech lead says 'we'd have to think about that.' Meanwhile, the lead PM last built something herself eight months ago and can't explain why her last three engineering requests were scoped the way they were. This team is staffed and skilled for a pre-composability era: builders who can only describe, engineers who can only implement, and no one owning the surface area where AI or non-engineers could safely generate UI.

frameworks.name: The Front-End Fork
frameworks.description: A two-path classification for front-end engineers choosing their career trajectory as AI compresses implementation work — composability work versus the handcrafted specialist lane.
when_to_apply: I'm a front-end developer and AI tools are handling more and more of what I used to do — where should I invest my time?
We're restructuring our front-end team and need to figure out which roles are about building design systems versus which are about pixel-level craft
I love the craft of building beautiful UI, but I'm worried it's becoming a niche — should I pivot or lean in?
As a manager, how do I create career ladders for front-end engineers when AI is compressing implementation work?
I'm a senior front-end engineer and I can't tell if my skills are becoming more valuable or less — the signals are contradictory
principles: Path 1 (Composability): Accept less direct making in exchange for more leverage over how making happens at scale
Path 2 (Handcrafted): Remain in implementation craft, which is becoming a specialist niche rather than the default path — choose it deliberately
Existing craft knowledge is essential context for composability work, not obsolete — knowing which decisions need locking requires having seen what happens when they aren't
Choosing neither path deliberately means drifting into obsolescence by default

source_posts.title: The Composability Era: What Happens When Anyone Can Build a UI (+ 4 Prompts to navigate the front-end revolution)

frameworks.example_application: This engineer has spent eight years perfecting CSS animations and accessible component APIs — that's Path 2, handcrafted specialist work. The critical question is whether they're choosing it deliberately. Right now their team is adopting AI-generated components for 70% of new surfaces, which means their craft is migrating from 'default expectation' to 'specialist niche.' If they stay, they need to own the quality ceiling — the work AI can't reach — and price accordingly. If they'd rather have leverage over the whole system, they shift to Path 1: building the design tokens, component constraints, and composability guardrails that make AI-generated UI consistently good. Their existing craft knowledge isn't wasted in that move — it's the exact context needed to know which decisions must be locked down versus left flexible. What they cannot do is stand still and assume the default path still exists.

frameworks.name: Delegation Spec Drill
frameworks.description: A weekly practice for building the skill of translating implicit work intentions into explicit, executable specifications that can be delegated to an agent or human.
when_to_apply: I keep getting back work from my AI agent that misses the point, and I suspect the problem is my instructions, not the model
I want to start delegating recurring tasks but I'm not sure which ones I can actually hand off versus which ones live in my head
I wrote a prompt or brief for someone and it generated more clarifying questions than actual output
I'm trying to build a weekly habit of getting better at specification writing for AI-assisted work
A task I delegated created more cleanup work than if I'd just done it myself
principles: A spec is only good if a stranger can execute it without questions
Success criteria must be binary, not subjective
Constraints must be explicit rather than implied
Approvals must be placed at reversibility boundaries — moments where actions become hard to undo
Failure handling must be specified for each step
Score 3 or below means the spec would create more work than it saves; 4 or 5 means it's delegation-ready
steps: Pick one task from the past week that took more than 30 minutes
Write the specification you would have needed to delegate it to someone who knows nothing about your context
Define Inputs: What information or access is required to start?
Define Steps: What sequence of actions produces the output?
Define Constraints: What must be true about the output, and what must not happen?
Define Approvals: Where would you need to sign off? Place these at reversibility boundaries.
Define Failure Handling: What happens if something goes wrong at each step?

Score the spec on five points: (1) Can a stranger execute it without questions? (2) Are success criteria binary? (3) Are constraints explicit rather than implied? (4) Are approvals at reversibility boundaries? (5) Is failure handling specified?

source_posts.title: Grab the Delegation Kit I Use to Turn AI into my Chief of Staff + the 8 Prompts That Turn Ramblings into Executable Tasks

frameworks.example_application: The task was 'research competitors and summarize findings' — took 90 minutes last Tuesday. The draft spec scored 2/5: steps were vague ('look at their websites'), success criteria were subjective ('a good summary'), constraints were entirely implied (didn't specify which competitors, what dimensions to compare, or output format), and failure handling was nonexistent. The spec would have generated more back-and-forth than it saved. Rewriting with binary success criteria ('table comparing 5 named competitors on pricing, integrations, and target segment, with source URLs for each cell') and explicit constraints ('no competitors under $1M ARR, no blog posts as sources') brought it to 4/5 — delegation-ready for an agent or junior analyst.

frameworks.name: The 30-Minute Delegation Rule
frameworks.description: A three-condition filter for determining whether a task is worth delegating at all, based on recurrence, duration, and batchability.
when_to_apply: I keep delegating small tasks to my AI assistant and spending more time reviewing the output than it would take to just do it
I'm building a list of tasks to automate or delegate and need to filter out the ones that aren't worth the setup cost
A task feels like it should be delegated but it's a one-time thing and I'm not sure the overhead is justified
I want a quick litmus test before writing a detailed delegation spec or prompt for an AI agent
My weekly review keeps surfacing tasks that could theoretically be delegated but I'm not sure which ones actually should be
principles: If you're doing a task once, don't delegate it — just do it
Delegation only pays off when the task recurs (instructions will be reused), takes longer than the delegation overhead, or can be batched with similar items
The goal is not to delegate everything, but to delegate the right things — systematic, repeatable, verifiable work that doesn't require your judgment
steps: Ask: Does this task recur? If no, do it yourself.
Ask: Does this task take longer than the delegation overhead (specification + review + correction)? If no, do it yourself.
Ask: Can this task be batched with similar items? If none of the three conditions are met, do it yourself.
If one or more conditions are met, proceed to write a delegation spec.

source_posts.title: Grab the Delegation Kit I Use to Turn AI into my Chief of Staff + the 8 Prompts That Turn Ramblings into Executable Tasks

frameworks.example_application: Formatting a one-off investor report fails all three conditions: it won't recur (this is a custom request), it takes 20 minutes (less than writing the spec, reviewing, and correcting), and there's nothing to batch it with. Do it yourself. But the weekly metrics summary passes two conditions — it recurs every Monday and can be batched with the other three weekly reporting tasks. That's worth a delegation spec.

frameworks.name: Delegation Scope Expansion Model
frameworks.description: A classification system that maps how the nature of delegatable work fundamentally changes at each order-of-magnitude expansion of AI time-horizon capability (tasks → projects → initiatives → judgment).
when_to_apply: I'm trying to figure out which parts of a large project I can delegate to AI versus which I need to do myself
My team is jumping straight to complex agent workflows without mastering simpler AI delegation first
I need to plan what AI delegation skills to invest in now versus what I can learn later as capabilities improve
I delegated a multi-phase project to an AI agent and it fell apart — I'm trying to understand why the same approach that works for simple tasks failed here
I'm designing oversight and review processes for AI-generated work and need to calibrate how much supervision different types of work require
principles: A five-hour delegatable task is not a scaled-down forty-hour task — each horizon represents a qualitatively different kind of work
Each horizon expansion opens entirely new categories of work, not just more of the same
Skills to delegate effectively at each level build on prior levels — practitioners who skip levels start from scratch
The distinction between delegating work and delegating judgment starts to blur at the forty-hour horizon
steps: Five-hour horizon: delegate discrete tasks with clear boundaries, single-session work, verifiable against explicit success criteria
Ten-hour horizon: delegate projects requiring planning, multiple phases, and synthesis — agent must make sequencing decisions and maintain coherence
Twenty-hour horizon: delegate initiatives spanning multiple work sessions — requires agent judgment about prioritization, not just execution
Forty-hour horizon: delegate judgment-laden work (business plans, audits, book-length drafts) where dependencies and decision points blur the line between work and judgment

source_posts.title: My honest field notes on the super-exponential + why "I'll catch up later" is now the riskiest bet

frameworks.example_application: A team lead wants to delegate a competitive analysis.
