At the five-hour horizon, the AI can research a single competitor and produce a structured summary — discrete, verifiable, bounded. At the twenty-hour horizon, the AI could run the full competitive landscape scan across twelve players, deciding which dimensions matter most and how to weight conflicting signals — that's an initiative requiring prioritization judgment, not just execution. The team lead who hasn't built the skill of specifying and verifying five-hour tasks will fail catastrophically at the twenty-hour delegation because the specification and oversight muscles are qualitatively different, not just scaled up.

frameworks.name: The Reversibility Gap
frameworks.description: Reframes AI agent deployment failures as a reversibility problem rather than an intelligence problem — agents fail in production not because they aren't smart enough, but because most business environments weren't designed to make mistakes survivable.
when_to_apply: My agent works great in demos but keeps causing problems in production that require manual cleanup
We're debating whether to wait for a better model before deploying agents, or ship now with the current one
I need to figure out why agents work well in software engineering but keep failing in our operations/finance/HR workflows
We're planning what infrastructure to build before giving our agents more autonomy
Leadership is asking why our agent made an irreversible mistake and I need to explain what went wrong structurally
principles: The limiting factor for agent deployment is reversibility of mistakes, not agent intelligence
Environments designed for safe failure (like software engineering) enable agent autonomy; environments that weren't designed that way resist it
The path to agent autonomy runs through reversibility infrastructure, not model capability improvements
Humans have been providing an informal safety throttle that disappears when agents replace them — this must be explicitly replaced
Boring, predictable, bounded, recoverable agent operations are the goal, not sophisticated ones

source_posts.title: Executive Briefing: Five Primitives That Make Agent Operations Safe

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that the customer service agent fails because it hallucinates refund policies — it needs a better model. That's wrong here. The real problem is that when the agent issues a refund incorrectly, there's no automated clawback, no staged approval, no transaction hold. A human agent making the same mistake would have caught it mid-process or a supervisor would have reversed it within the hour — that informal safety net was never formalized. The fix isn't GPT-5; it's a 15-minute refund hold with automatic review triggers. The environment needs reversibility infrastructure, not more intelligence.

frameworks.name: The Jagged Frontier Framework
frameworks.description: A classification system for mapping AI capability peaks and valleys across tasks, then routing work to match AI's structural advantages while humans cover failure modes.
when_to_apply: AI works great for some tasks in my workflow but produces garbage for seemingly similar ones, and I can't figure out the pattern
We're getting inconsistent results from an AI deployment and need to figure out which pieces to keep vs. pull back to humans
Some people on my team get massive productivity gains from AI while others doing similar work see almost nothing — what explains the gap?
I need to decide which parts of a process to automate with AI vs. keep human-led, and 'try it and see' isn't a strategy
Our AI pilot showed impressive demos but real-world performance is disappointing and we need to diagnose why
principles: AI capability surfaces are jagged, not smooth — peaks and valleys coexist on adjacent tasks
Misuse outside the frontier doesn't just fail to help — it actively degrades outcomes
The 30% gains crowd treats AI as a power tool (more output, same shape of work); the 300% gains crowd treats AI as a routing layer (redesigned workflows matching AI's structural advantages)
Fluency means navigating jaggedness intentionally, not just generating more AI output
Each deployment surface has its own failure modes — a failure in one context doesn't predict failure in another
Map tasks into three zones: AI reliably better, AI reliably worse, and high variance
steps: Inventory your tasks and map each into one of three zones: AI reliably better, AI reliably worse, high variance
Identify which tasks sit inside vs. outside the AI frontier for your specific context
Redesign workflows so AI handles tasks in the 'reliably better' zone and humans cover edge cases and failure modes
Build evaluation harnesses and 'known failure mode' checklists per workflow to catch regressions
Continuously update the map as capability thresholds shift

source_posts.title: NEW: One Google Update Spawned 3 Startup Generations in 30 Days—Here's the Pattern + 4 Prompts to Position Before the Next Cascade

frameworks.example_application: A legal team getting 'mixed results' from AI contract review has been treating all contract tasks as one block. Mapping the jagged frontier reveals: extracting standard clause language and flagging missing sections sit inside the frontier (AI reliably better — faster, more consistent). But evaluating whether a non-standard indemnification clause is commercially acceptable in this deal's context sits firmly outside it (AI reliably worse — it generates confident but wrong risk assessments). The team redesigned: AI handles extraction and completeness checks, humans handle commercial judgment calls, and the high-variance zone — summarizing negotiation history — gets AI drafts with mandatory human review. That routing shift moved them from marginal gains to transformative ones, not by using AI more, but by using it only where the frontier map says it wins.

frameworks.name: Cascade Scanner / Gap-Close Pattern
frameworks.description: A structured approach to identifying which AI capability gaps are about to close and predicting the downstream business cascade that will follow, by analyzing what building blocks already exist versus what single unlock is missing.
when_to_apply: A new foundation model just dropped and I'm trying to figure out if it's incremental or if it crosses a threshold that unlocks entire product categories
I can see that 90% of the building blocks for a capability exist but deployment is still stuck — what's the actual blocker and when does it break?
I want to place bets on where to build before the next wave of AI startups becomes obvious to everyone
I'm scanning adjacent AI capability areas to decide which gap-close would create the most downstream opportunity for my company
Multiple AI capabilities seem close to usable but none have broken through to mass adoption yet — which one tips first?
principles: You don't need to improve the entire AI capability surface — you only need to fill in the right gap
Look for areas where almost all building blocks exist but one specific component is missing
A gap closes faster when distribution infrastructure is already in place (pipes already laid)
The question for each area is: what exists now, what's missing, and what would a real breakthrough look like?
When a capability crosses the usability threshold plus hits broad distribution simultaneously, the cascade happens in weeks not years
Three lineages tend to light up at once when a shared missing piece is filled: consumer creation, knowledge-work collateral, and professional tooling
steps: Identify a capability area where progress is happening but deployment is still blocked
Enumerate what building blocks already exist (models, infrastructure, distribution surfaces)
Identify the single specific gap that is acting as the hard blocker
Assess whether distribution infrastructure is already in place to propagate a breakthrough
Predict the downstream cascade: which product categories unlock the moment the gap closes
Position or build before the threshold is crossed, not after the cascade is visible

source_posts.title: NEW: One Google Update Spawned 3 Startup Generations in 30 Days—Here's the Pattern + 4 Prompts to Position Before the Next Cascade

frameworks.example_application: Real-time video understanding already has strong models (GPT-4V, Gemini), cloud infrastructure, and billions of camera-equipped devices as distribution surfaces. The single missing piece is sub-second multimodal inference at consumer-grade cost. The moment that threshold is crossed — likely within one model generation — three lineages ignite simultaneously: consumer apps (real-time AR translation, cooking coaches), knowledge-work collateral (auto-generated meeting summaries with visual context), and professional tooling (quality inspection, surgical assist). The distribution pipes are already laid through existing mobile OS integrations, so adoption will cascade in weeks. Building the harness layer now — before the unlock is visible — is the only way to capture position.

frameworks.name: Model + Y + X Framework (The Harnessing Layer)
frameworks.description: Reframes the conventional wisdom that AI competitive advantage = Model + Domain Expertise, by inserting a critical middle variable 'Y' (the harnessing layer of system design, validation, and constraint enforcement) that determines whether domain expertise actually gets leveraged.
when_to_apply: We have better domain experts than our competitors but our AI product still underperforms theirs
Our AI demos are impressive but we can't get the system to work reliably at scale in production
We're debating whether to invest in model fine-tuning vs. building validation and error-handling infrastructure
Leadership keeps saying 'we have proprietary data' as our moat but our actual outputs aren't better than competitors using the same base model
Our team has deep expertise but can't figure out why the AI system doesn't reflect that knowledge in its outputs
principles: Domain expertise (X) alone is insufficient—it stays theoretical without a harnessing layer
Y (the harnessing layer) is the multiplier that unlocks X
The harnessing layer includes validation logic, routing, constraint enforcement, repair steps, and failure instrumentation
Teams that ship are the ones who built Y, not the ones with the best models or most resources
The messy middle integration layer is underbuilt and represents the primary opportunity

source_posts.title: 9 bets I'm making on AI in 2026 + the audit I use to spot real systems

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that Company A wins because they have deeper clinical expertise and fine-tuned models. That's wrong here — Company B ships reliable results with a generic model because they built the harnessing layer: validation logic that catches hallucinated drug interactions, routing that escalates ambiguous cases, constraint enforcement that blocks outputs violating formulary rules, and repair steps that auto-correct common failure patterns. Company A's domain expertise is theoretical — it lives in their team's heads, not in executable system logic. The multiplier is zero without Y, so Model × 0 × X = 0 no matter how good X is.

frameworks.name: The Devil's Game (Friction Trade-off)
frameworks.description: Reframes AI product design tensions not as solvable UX problems but as structurally irreconcilable trade-offs, where the design choices that win consumer adoption actively undermine enterprise delegation capability.
when_to_apply: Our employees love ChatGPT personally but our enterprise AI deployment keeps failing on governance and accountability
We're debating whether to wait for our AI vendor to add enterprise features or build internal governance tooling ourselves
Why does adding verification and oversight to our AI workflows always tank user adoption?
Our AI vendor keeps promising enterprise capabilities but the product keeps optimizing for consumer speed and simplicity
We're trying to understand whether consumer AI adoption is helping or hurting our enterprise AI strategy
principles: Making delegation legible requires friction (work orders, verification, visible cost, slower execution)
Consumer distribution punishes friction — speed and simplicity drive retention at scale
These two optimization targets are not just in tension; product decisions that win one game actively teach the wrong mental model for the other
The same product walks into the enterprise through consumer adoption, embedding the wrong mental model before enterprise tooling can correct it

source_posts.title: Executive Briefing: The Bubble Test for OpenAI (Unit Economics, Capacity, Proof—Three Signals to Watch in 2026)

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that ChatGPT's consumer simplicity is a stepping stone to enterprise readiness — just add admin controls and audit logs. That's wrong here because the core product teaches users that AI interaction is instant, frictionless, and requires no specification of intent. Every employee who adopts the consumer product internalizes that mental model before IT can deploy enterprise governance. The friction required for delegatable AI — work orders, verification steps, visible cost signals, slower execution with audit trails — isn't a feature gap to close; it's a design direction that directly contradicts what made the consumer product successful. The company isn't failing to serve enterprise; it's structurally incapable of optimizing for both without forking the product.

frameworks.name: Work Primitives
frameworks.description: A four-dimension assessment of whether an organization's work structure is legible enough for AI agents to operate on, determining whether agent leverage can actually be captured.
when_to_apply: We bought Copilot licenses for the whole team but adoption is flat and nobody can explain why
I want to deploy AI agents on our workflows but I'm not sure which processes are actually ready
Our AI tools give good advice but nothing actually gets done automatically — there's always a human copy-pasting
We're a non-technical team wondering what we'd need to change about how we work before AI agents could help
Why does our competitor seem to get 10x from AI while we're stuck at 1.2x despite using the same models?
principles: Agent leverage requires work to be structured in materials that agents can read and act on — not locked in human heads or opaque admin panels
The four primitives are necessary preconditions for delegation, whether to humans or agents
Organizations that lack these primitives will be limited to an advisory layer with capable models but limited actual impact
These are not coding skills — they are structural properties of how work is organized
Rollback capability is what makes high throughput safe, not just fast

source_posts.title: Inside OpenAI's Codex Team: Always-On AI Feedback, Everyone Commits Code, No One Cares About Titles—A Look at the Future of Work + 6 Prompts to Make it Real in Your Business

frameworks.example_application: This team scores poorly on all four primitives. Tasks live in Slack threads and verbal handoffs (no machine-readable task definitions), artifacts are created in admin panels with no API (no programmatic access), there's no version control on their core deliverables (no rollback capability), and completion criteria are 'the manager looks at it and says it's done' (no verifiable done state). The model they deployed is GPT-4-class — plenty capable — but it's reduced to a chat assistant because there's nothing structured for it to operate on. Restructuring the work primitives is the prerequisite; upgrading the model is irrelevant until then.

frameworks.name: Moving Goalposts Failure Pattern
frameworks.description: Enumerates the progressive, unacknowledged redefinition of 'correct' that occurs in AI projects, where each stakeholder layer adds undocumented requirements until the team is effectively building multiple different products without realizing it.
when_to_apply: Our AI outputs used to be fine but now everyone's unhappy and nobody can explain what changed
Different stakeholders keep rejecting the same AI output for completely different reasons
Engineering says they met the spec but the business side says the product is broken
We keep adding 'small tweaks' to what the AI should produce and each sprint feels like starting over
My personal AI workflow that used to feel great now feels inadequate even though I haven't changed the prompts
principles: Correctness redefinition happens silently — each change feels like a minor adjustment but the aggregate shift is a new product
The AI is not becoming less reliable; human standards are shifting without acknowledgment
Each stakeholder layer adds requirements without removing or reconciling prior ones
The failure is upstream in human specification, not in model performance
Catching this pattern requires naming what you want, noticing when it changes, and updating specifications explicitly

source_posts.title: I've reviewed 20+ enterprise AI builds this year—they all skip this conversation + 7 prompts that force it before anyone writes code

frameworks.example_application: The team says the model's summarization quality has 'degraded' over three sprints, but no model changes were made. The real timeline: Sprint 1, the PM defined 'correct' as factually accurate summaries. Sprint 2, Legal added a requirement that summaries must flag liability language — never written down, communicated verbally in a review meeting. Sprint 3, the CFO rejected outputs that didn't include financial impact estimates, which no one had ever specified. The team is now building three products — a summarizer, a legal risk scanner, and a financial impact estimator — under the label of one. The model isn't failing; it's being evaluated against a specification that doesn't exist yet.

frameworks.name: Work Delegation Bucket Classification
frameworks.description: A three-category classification of work types for deciding how to approach AI delegation, based on whether the work is new, high-value existing, or tedious recurring.
when_to_apply: I have a dozen tasks I could try with AI but I don't know which ones to start with
I'm worried about AI making mistakes on important work but I also don't want to over-verify everything
Some of my work is brand new exploration and some is repetitive drudgery — should I treat them the same when delegating to AI?
I want to build an AI delegation habit but need a way to calibrate how much I trust the output for different task types
My team is adopting AI tools and we need a simple framework for which tasks get full autonomy versus careful review
principles: New work (tasks never completed before) has low downside risk — any progress is a win, so it is safe to experiment freely
High-value existing work requires careful baseline comparison — verify that AI output improves on what you'd produce yourself before trusting it
Tedious recurring work is the safest and most immediately valuable target — spot-checking quickly reveals model quality with low stakes
steps: Classify the task: Is this new work that has never been done? High-value existing work with a known baseline? Or tedious recurring work?
For new work: gather available data and delegate freely — any output is net-positive progress
For high-value existing work: delegate with careful data preparation, then compare output to your baseline to assess quality before relying on it
For tedious recurring work: delegate and spot-check — quality is easy to assess and the leverage is immediate

source_posts.title: NEW: ChatGPT 5.2 Complete Teardown—I tested Excel, PowerPoint, and 10,000-row datasets—Here's My Take, Comparison vs. Opus 4.5 and Gemini 3 + 15 Prompts to Power Up GPT 5.2

frameworks.example_application: This weekly client report is tedious recurring work — same structure, same data sources, same format every Friday. That makes it the highest-leverage delegation target: hand it to the model, spot-check two or three outputs against last week's reports, and if quality holds, it's automated. The strategic competitor analysis the CEO requested, on the other hand, is new work that's never been done before — there's no baseline to beat, so any structured output is a net win worth experimenting with freely. But rewriting the pricing model — that's high-value existing work where the team already has a vetted spreadsheet. Delegating that requires running the AI output side-by-side against the current model and verifying every formula before trusting it.

frameworks.name: Five Core Knowledge Work Skills (Plus One to Argue Against)
frameworks.description: A classification of the five recurring skills that determine knowledge worker effectiveness — Judgment, Orchestration, Coordination, Taste, and Updating — each defined by its artifact surface and characteristic failure mode, plus an argument against treating 'prompting' as a top-level skill.
when_to_apply: Designing a rubric for evaluating knowledge worker output beyond surface-level writing quality
My team keeps producing mediocre documents and I can't pinpoint whether it's a skills gap or a process gap
We're debating whether to invest in prompt engineering training or something more fundamental
Building promotion criteria or job descriptions that reflect what actually makes someone effective, not just their title
Deciding which skills to target in a deliberate practice program for knowledge workers
principles: Skills live in artifacts — the documents you leave behind — not in job titles or LinkedIn taglines
Each skill has a characteristic failure mode that is observable in written output
Orchestration and specification literacy are the deeper skills that make prompting work — train those instead
Updating is visible in how positions evolve over time, not in how they are defended
Taste requires being able to articulate what 'good' looks like, not just recognize it

source_posts.title: Grab the 9 prompts I use to turn docs into practice reps + a 90-day pilot you can steal

frameworks.example_application: This team's quarterly planning docs keep getting sent back for revision, and the instinct is to blame 'communication skills.' But the artifacts tell a different story. The plans show strong coordination (stakeholders are mapped, dependencies noted) and decent taste (the format and structure are clean). The failure is in judgment — every plan treats three competing priorities as equally important, never making the hard call about what to cut. That's not a writing problem; it's a judgment deficit that shows up in writing. The development investment should target judgment practice reps, not another 'better business writing' course. And the request to add 'prompt engineering' training is a distraction — what these people actually lack is specification literacy and orchestration skill, which are the deeper capabilities that make any tool (including AI) produce better output.

frameworks.name: Two Memory Problems Distinction
frameworks.description: Separates two commonly conflated agent memory failure modes—cross-session amnesia (domain memory) and within-session degradation (context engineering)—clarifying that they have different causes and require different architectural solutions.
when_to_apply: An agent loses progress between conversation sessions but works fine within a single session
An agent starts sharp but becomes confused or repetitive deep into a long task
We added persistent memory files but the agent still degrades mid-task — what are we missing?
Evaluating whether an agent vendor's 'memory' feature solves cross-session continuity, within-session coherence, or both
Trying to figure out whether confused agent behavior is a storage problem or a context window management problem
principles: Domain memory (cross-session): the agent has no persistent record of where things stand; each session starts fresh; solved by structured external records (task lists, progress logs, validation criteria)
Context engineering (within-session): the agent accumulates too much in the context window mid-task, burying critical signal under noise; solved by computed views and active state management
Both problems are necessary to solve; external records without context engineering still produces mid-session degradation
Context engineering without domain memory means every session starts without continuity even if the session itself stays coherent
The two failure modes look similar (confused, forgetting things) but have completely different root causes and fixes

source_posts.title: Get the Cheat Code on Long-Running AI Agents—Here's What Manus, Google, and Anthropic Learned After Trial and Error + 12 Prompts to Help Build Long-Running Agents Yourself

frameworks.example_application: This team added a task log and progress file between sessions, but the agent still goes off the rails 40 minutes into complex multi-step work. That's not a domain memory problem — the agent starts each session knowing exactly where it left off. The failure is context engineering: mid-session, the context window fills with raw tool outputs, prior reasoning traces, and accumulated conversation history until the critical constraints get buried. The fix isn't better external records — it's computed views that surface only the active task state, validation criteria, and relevant constraints instead of dumping the full session history into the window.

frameworks.name: λ/Δ/θ Focus Capacity Model
frameworks.description: A three-variable model that quantifies deep work capacity by measuring interruption rate (λ), recovery time (Δ), and minimum viable work block size (θ), then calculating how many meaningful work units fit into a given day.
when_to_apply: I feel like I'm busy all day but can't point to a single meaningful thing I accomplished
I'm trying to decide whether to accept another recurring meeting and want to know the real cost to my deep work
My team complains they never have time for real work despite having 'open' calendars
I had a terrible productivity day and want to pinpoint whether it was interruptions, slow recovery, or too-small time blocks
I'm redesigning my team's Slack and meeting norms and need a quantitative model for how changes affect focus capacity
principles: Focus capacity is a function of measurable environmental variables, not willpower or character
Interruption rate (λ), recovery time (Δ), and minimum block size (θ) together determine whether deep work is statistically possible on a given day
Count real work units by asking how many θ-sized chunks fit into each focus block, rounding down — the rounding is harsh but honest
Small changes to any single variable can produce disproportionately large improvements in total capacity
Roughly half of interruptions are self-inflicted, making personal habit change as important as environmental design
If θ exceeds available block sizes, the result is constant thrashing regardless of total time spent working
steps: Establish your baseline λ: count how many times per hour your attention is pulled away (Slack, email, questions, pop-ups)
Establish your baseline Δ: estimate how many minutes it takes to mentally re-engage with deep work after each interruption
Establish your baseline θ: identify the minimum uninterrupted block length before you feel you've made meaningful progress on real work
Audit your calendar to identify your actual focus blocks — the stretches between scheduled interruptions
For each focus block, calculate how many θ-sized chunks fit inside it (rounding down), then sum across blocks to get your daily capacity
Identify which variable (λ, Δ, or θ) is the binding constraint on your current capacity
Apply targeted interventions: reduce λ via triage and async defaults, reduce Δ via context-capture habits, reduce θ via work decomposition

source_posts.title: The focus system I borrowed from an engineer's blog + 18 prompts to actually move the dials

frameworks.example_application: A senior engineer has 8 hours of nominal work time but gets interrupted roughly 4 times per hour (λ=4), takes about 15 minutes to re-engage each time (Δ=15), and needs at least 45-minute blocks to make meaningful progress on architecture work (θ=45). After mapping scheduled meetings and calculating interruption-fragmented gaps, only 2 blocks per day exceed 45 minutes — yielding exactly 2 deep work units. That's not a motivation problem; it's arithmetic. The binding constraint is λ: cutting interruptions from 4/hour to 2/hour by batching Slack into 30-minute check windows would nearly double usable capacity without touching the calendar at all.

frameworks.name: Task Decomposition Framework
frameworks.description: A structured method for breaking any workflow into atomic, AI-ready tasks by identifying cognitive type, matching model capabilities, and routing each sub-task to the most appropriate tool rather than applying one model to the entire workflow.
when_to_apply: I'm trying to automate a complex knowledge work process and my single-prompt approach keeps producing mediocre results that need heavy editing
My team uses one AI model for everything and I suspect we're overpaying for simple tasks while underserving complex ones
I need to design an AI workflow but the process involves very different types of thinking — some parts need precision, others need creativity
We want to move from ad-hoc AI usage to a repeatable, teachable methodology our whole team can follow
I'm building a multi-step AI pipeline and need to figure out which model to assign to which step
principles: Map what humans actually do step-by-step before designing any AI workflow
Identify each distinct cognitive operation as a separate task, not as part of a single prompt
Match each task to the cognitive type category it belongs to (extraction, synthesis, analysis, generation, validation)
Assign models based on the cognitive type and the specific requirements of that task
Treat the cost question as a math problem: measure time saved versus cost of additional tools
Intuition for which model fits which task can only be built through deliberate, tracked experimentation — not documentation
Professional-looking output is not a signal of correctness; validate outputs against the actual requirements of each task type
steps: Map the workflow by documenting every distinct step a skilled human performs, not the high-level description of the deliverable
Identify the cognitive type for each step (extraction, synthesis, analysis, generation, or validation)
Note the specific requirements of each task — precision needs, context volume, style consistency, rule complexity
Match each task to a model suited to that cognitive type and those specific requirements
Run deliberate experiments routing the same tasks to different models and tracking quality outcomes
Build the multi-model pipeline with each task routed to its matched model
Calculate actual cost versus time saved to validate the approach economically

source_posts.title: My honest field notes on why AI implementations fail at the task level + the 10 prompt templates I built to fix it
This is The First Year AI Can Shop Black Friday But There are NO Prompts—So I Fixed That With 6 Black Friday Prompts to Save You Hundreds

frameworks.example_application: A consulting firm's report-writing process actually decomposes into five distinct cognitive operations: extracting key metrics from client data (extraction), identifying patterns across quarters (analysis), synthesizing findings into a narrative (synthesis), generating client-facing prose (generation), and checking claims against source data (validation). Extraction and validation demand precision — a smaller, cheaper model with structured output handles these reliably. Synthesis and generation require nuance and style consistency — that's frontier model territory. Analysis sits in between and needs experimentation to route correctly. Running all five through GPT-4 costs 4x what the multi-model pipeline costs, and the single-model approach actually performs worse on extraction because the model over-elaborates instead of returning clean structured data.

frameworks.name: Accuracy vs. Intelligence Failure Distinction
frameworks.description: A diagnostic distinction between two fundamentally different AI failure modes — precision errors in rule application versus absence of contextual judgment — that produce identical symptoms (professional-looking but useless output) but require different fixes.
when_to_apply: My AI draft has all the right data but an expert would say it completely misses the point
I'm trying to decide whether to fix my prompt, switch models, or redesign how I've broken down the task
Two different AI workflows are both producing useless output and I need to figure out if they're failing for the same reason
The AI's analysis is technically correct but reads like it was written by someone who has never worked in this domain
My outputs only reveal their problems when a subject matter expert reviews them — they pass surface-level checks fine
principles: Both failure modes produce the same symptom: professional-looking output that misses the point
Accuracy failures occur when a model applies rules or calculations incorrectly — a precision problem fixable by better model selection or task isolation
Intelligence failures occur when a model lacks the contextual judgment to interpret what correct data means — a reasoning problem requiring different task design
Diagnosing the correct failure type before redesigning a workflow prevents solving the wrong problem
A model can count without being able to see — statistical correctness and interpretive insight are separate capabilities

source_posts.title: My honest field notes on why AI implementations fail at the task level + the 10 prompt templates I built to fix it

frameworks.example_application: The financial summary the model produced has correct revenue figures and accurate growth percentages, but it completely missed that the growth is coming from a single customer who represents 60% of revenue — a concentration risk any analyst would flag immediately. This is an intelligence failure, not an accuracy failure. The numbers are right; the interpretation is absent. Switching to a better model won't fix this — the task needs to be restructured so that interpretive questions ('what does this data pattern mean for risk?') are separated from data extraction, and domain-specific judgment criteria are injected into the prompt as explicit evaluation lenses.

frameworks.name: Edge-First Automation Framework
frameworks.description: Reframes AI workflow automation strategy by targeting the mechanical periphery (data prep, QA, synthesis, packaging, coordination) before the high-judgment core, to reduce failure risk and build organizational trust.
when_to_apply: We tried to automate a complex workflow end-to-end and the project stalled or people lost confidence in it
My team wants to use AI agents but we're not sure which part of the process to target first
Stakeholders are skeptical about AI automation because a previous attempt broke something that worked fine before
We have a high-judgment workflow surrounded by tedious manual steps and I need to figure out the sequencing
Our AI automation project keeps expanding in scope and we need a principled way to constrain it
principles: Start with the edges (data prep, QA, synthesis, packaging, coordination) before touching the core
Core workflows contain hidden complexity, tribal knowledge, and judgment that current models reliably underestimate
Automation is an organizational trust exercise, not just a technical project — losing trust locks away the tribal knowledge you need
Early wins should be fast (one to two weeks), semi-manual, and designed to capture 70-80% of cases while routing exceptions to humans
Automate around human expertise, not through it — protect the craft by eliminating the tedium surrounding it
Each edge automated builds the infrastructure, exception maps, and trust needed to eventually approach the core
Do not attempt core automation until inputs are clean, edge-to-core boundaries are clear, exceptions are visible, operators trust the system, and edge automations run stably
steps: Pick a workflow you touch every week that matters to you or your team
Map the five edge categories: data preparation, QA, synthesis, packaging, and coordination
Identify where time and energy disappear in the pre- and post-core phases
Select the simplest edge — not the most impressive, but the one with the fastest, clearest lift
Build a semi-manual version-0 that automates the predictable 70-80% and flags the rest for human review
Ship, observe real usage, and iterate based on what exceptions surface
Stack multiple successful edge automations before assessing readiness to approach the core
Run a readiness check on five dimensions before moving inward: clean inputs, clear edge-core boundary, visible exceptions, operator trust, and stable edge automations

source_posts.title: I Finally Cracked Why AI Agent Projects Keep Failing—And I Built a Workbook with 11 Prompts So You Can Fix Yours Tomorrow

frameworks.example_application: The conventional instinct is to automate the core underwriting decision — that's where the most labor-intensive judgment sits, so it looks like the biggest win. That's wrong here because the underwriting team's real pain isn't the decision itself; it's the 6 hours per case spent gathering documents, normalizing data formats, and chasing brokers for missing fields. Those are edges — data prep and coordination — where 80% of cases follow a predictable pattern. Automating those first delivers immediate time savings, builds the team's trust that AI handles their inputs reliably, and surfaces the exception patterns (incomplete appraisals, non-standard property types) that any future core automation would need to handle anyway.

frameworks.name: Five Edge Categories
frameworks.description: A classification system for the five types of automatable peripheral work that surround any high-judgment core workflow, used to systematically identify where to start an automation initiative.
when_to_apply: I can see that our team spends most of their time on stuff around the actual work, not the work itself, and I want to systematically catalog what's automatable
We're starting an automation initiative and need to prioritize which peripheral tasks to tackle first across a complex workflow
I keep hearing 'automate the edges' but I need a concrete taxonomy to make sure I'm identifying all the edge work, not just the obvious stuff
Our knowledge workers are drowning in prep work, QA, and formatting — I need to classify these tasks to build a sequenced automation roadmap
I want to audit a workflow to find where current LLM capabilities can actually deliver value without requiring deep domain judgment
principles: Data preparation: collecting, cleaning, normalizing, and reconciling inputs before the core work begins
QA: verifying completeness, consistency, and absence of obvious errors — automatable without understanding the full workflow
Synthesis: summarizing, consolidating, or translating information from sprawling sources into actionable formats
Packaging: transforming finished work into the required deliverable format for the next stage
Coordination: moving context between systems or people, eliminating the human translation layer in handoffs
All five categories share the profile of low-judgment, well-defined outputs, and inputs that are already ready — making them suitable for automation even with imperfect models

source_posts.title: I Finally Cracked Why AI Agent Projects Keep Failing—And I Built a Workbook with 11 Prompts So You Can Fix Yours Tomorrow

frameworks.example_application: A legal team's contract review process has five distinct edge categories consuming human hours. Data preparation — pulling clause libraries and prior agreements from three different systems — takes 40% of paralegal time. Synthesis — consolidating redline comments from four stakeholders into a single change summary — takes another 25%. Both are low-judgment, well-defined-output tasks with inputs already available. Packaging (reformatting final agreements into client-specific templates) and coordination (emailing status updates between internal counsel and outside firms) round out the automation surface. QA on formatting consistency is trivially automatable. The core judgment — whether a clause creates unacceptable risk — stays human. Starting with data preparation yields the highest time savings with the lowest verification burden.

frameworks.name: Core Automation Readiness Check
frameworks.description: A five-dimension readiness assessment that determines whether a team has earned the right to automate a workflow's high-judgment core after successfully automating its edges.
when_to_apply: We've had some wins automating the simpler parts of our workflow and leadership wants us to automate the high-judgment center next
Our last attempt to automate the core decision-making step of a process failed and we're trying to understand why
The team is debating whether to start an automation project at the most valuable step or work inward from the periphery
Edge automations are running but I'm not sure the preconditions are actually met to go deeper
Operators who do the core work are skeptical of expanding automation scope and I need to assess whether their concerns are legitimate
principles: Rushing the core before preconditions are met costs more time than waiting
All five dimensions must be satisfied — partial readiness is not readiness
Readiness is earned through successful edge automation, not assumed from technical capability
steps: Assess whether inputs to the core are now clean and reliable (from edge automation of data prep)
Assess whether the boundary between edge work and core work is clearly defined
Assess whether exceptions that were previously invisible are now visible and mapped
Assess whether the operators who do the core work trust the automation system you have built
Assess whether your edge automations run stably without constant human intervention
If all five are yes, proceed to core automation; if any are no, continue building edges until they are

source_posts.title: I Finally Cracked Why AI Agent Projects Keep Failing—And I Built a Workbook with 11 Prompts So You Can Fix Yours Tomorrow

frameworks.example_application: The team's edge automations for data ingestion and formatting are running cleanly, and the boundary between prep work and underwriting judgment is well-defined. But the underwriters don't trust the system yet — they've been burned by silent failures twice — and the exception taxonomy is still incomplete (three new edge cases surfaced last week that nobody had mapped). Two of five dimensions fail. The right move is to keep running edges, build the exception map, and earn operator trust before touching core underwriting logic. Attempting core automation now would produce a system that looks functional in demos but collapses under real exception load.

frameworks.name: Prompt Lifecycle Diagnostic Checklist
frameworks.description: A branching symptom-to-stage mapping that helps practitioners locate where in the prompt lifecycle their problem actually lives, so they apply the right fix rather than the wrong tool.
when_to_apply: I've rewritten this prompt a dozen times and it's still not working — I don't know what else to try
My prompt works great in the playground but fails in production and I can't figure out why
Output quality from our agent has been degrading over the past few weeks even though we haven't changed the prompt
An agentic workflow is producing errors and I'm not sure if the issue is the prompt, the orchestration, or something else entirely
My team keeps applying prompt engineering tips but nothing improves — we might be fixing the wrong thing
principles: Match the symptom to the stage before reaching for a tool
Wordsmithing cannot fix an under-specified task — goal clarity must come before wording
Reliability drift is an evaluation problem, not a drafting problem
Production failures may live in orchestration or deployment layers, not in the prompt text itself
steps: Ask: Is the goal unclear or under-specified? → Stage 1 problem; define objectives, constraints, and output format before rewording
Ask: Is the wording messy or ambiguous despite clear intent? → Stage 2 problem; use drafting tools or optimizers
Ask: Is output reliability drifting across runs? → Stage 4 problem; build test cases and run evaluations
Ask: Is the prompt failing in production context? → Stage 5 or 6 problem; check orchestration logic, monitoring, and deployment configuration

source_posts.title: Prompting is Too Hard: Check Out My Easy Prompt Lifecycle Guide + 19 Prompting Tools + a Custom Prompt to Analyze your Prompting Strengths & Weaknesses

frameworks.example_application: The team has rewritten their summarization prompt twelve times, but outputs still vary wildly between runs. The wording is actually fine — the task specification is clear, the format is defined, and a single run produces good results. The real problem is Stage 4: there are no evaluation test cases, so they have no way to detect or measure the drift. They need a regression suite, not another prompt rewrite. The fix is to build five canonical input-output pairs and run automated checks, not to add more instructions to the system prompt.

frameworks.name: AI-Native Job Transformation Roadmap
frameworks.description: A four-step process for converting an existing knowledge-worker role into an AI-augmented role by mapping workflows, prototyping with approved tools, shipping a real use case, and integrating with organizational governance.
when_to_apply: I use AI tools at work but it still feels like toy demos — I want to ship something real that my team actually depends on
Our org is rolling out AI tooling and I want to be the person who shapes how it lands in my function, not the person it happens to
I'm a senior IC who needs to demonstrate AI workflow design credibility for my next performance cycle or job search
My manager asked me to figure out where AI fits in our team's workflows and I need a structured approach
I want to build a relationship with our AI governance team but I don't have anything concrete to show them yet
principles: Design the AI-native version of your job before someone else does it for you
AI augments structured, repetitive, verifiable work—not judgment-heavy or politically nuanced work
Work within approved organizational tools and security guardrails, not around them
Ship one real workflow that others rely on rather than accumulating toy demos
Pair business-side workflow knowledge with governance vocabulary to become a cross-functional bridge
The goal is to shift your value from executing work to supervising and designing workflows
steps: Step 1 — Map your work like a systems designer: Identify 3–5 recurring workflows you own and for each document the trigger, inputs, steps, decision points, outputs, verification checks, and exception handling

Step 2 — Learn to express those workflows to your existing approved AI tools: Give AI structured, scoped instructions; feed clean formatted inputs; request directly usable outputs; iterate until you have a stable, repeatable prompt recipe for each workflow

Step 3 — Ship an MVP of one meaningful AI-augmented workflow: Pick a high-frequency, painful, low-blast-radius workflow; automate 60–80% of the steps while keeping yourself in the loop for approval and exceptions; measure time saved, error rate, and throughput; document it as a one-pager with numbers

Step 4 — Build a relationship with whoever owns AI and platform governance in your org: Show your experiment as a responsible insider, ask what patterns they are standardizing, surface where they are nervous about AI in your function, and align your work to their highest-priority modernization targets

source_posts.title: Grab the AI Native Job Prompt—A Custom Guide to Make YOUR Role AI Native in 2026

frameworks.example_application: A marketing operations manager mapped five recurring workflows — campaign brief generation, performance report assembly, audience segmentation QA, creative asset tagging, and budget reallocation memos. The campaign brief workflow had the highest frequency, lowest blast radius, and clearest verification criteria (does the brief match the intake form plus historical performance data?). Automating 70% of brief generation with a stable prompt recipe inside the approved enterprise ChatGPT instance saved 6 hours per week across the team. Documenting that result as a one-pager with time-saved and error-rate numbers, then presenting it to the platform governance team, converted the manager from 'person who uses AI sometimes' into the go-to bridge between marketing and the AI modernization initiative — which is where durable career value lives.

frameworks.name: Workflow Decomposition API
frameworks.description: A structured method for making implicit job work explicit by breaking any recurring workflow into seven defined components, creating a 'mental API' for your own role that enables AI integration and process improvement.
when_to_apply: I keep asking AI to help with my job but the outputs are generic and miss the nuances of what I actually do
I need to onboard a new hire or document my role and I'm realizing how much of my process lives only in my head
My company is rolling out an AI initiative and I need to figure out which parts of my workflow are automatable vs. judgment-heavy
I want to build a custom GPT or AI assistant for my role but I don't know how to specify what it should do
I'm trying to figure out why AI tools work well for some of my tasks but completely fail on others
principles: Most knowledge workers have never made their own work explicit—doing so is itself a competitive advantage
If you cannot describe the work clearly enough to write it down, an AI model has no chance of helping with it
Making work explicit is the prerequisite to improving it, whether or not AI is involved
Every recurring job function can be decomposed into trigger, inputs, steps, decisions, outputs, verification, and exception handling
steps: Identify the trigger: what event or condition starts this workflow?
List the inputs: what information or resources do you need before you can begin?
Document the steps: what do you actually do, in order?
Mark the decision points: where do you make judgment calls and what criteria do you use?
Define the outputs: what do you produce at the end?
Specify verification: how do you check that the output is correct?
Define exception handling: what do you do when something goes wrong or an edge case appears?

source_posts.title: Grab the AI Native Job Prompt—A Custom Guide to Make YOUR Role AI Native in 2026

frameworks.example_application: A product manager says 'I want AI to help me write PRDs.' Running the decomposition reveals: the trigger is a prioritization decision from the roadmap review, the inputs are customer research summaries, engineering capacity estimates, and strategic goals, the steps include synthesizing competing signals into a single problem statement, the key decision point is scoping — choosing what to cut — using criteria like engineering cost, revenue impact, and strategic alignment, the output is a PRD with acceptance criteria, verification is a stakeholder review meeting where engineering confirms feasibility, and exception handling covers cases where dependencies on other teams invalidate assumptions mid-sprint. Now the actual AI integration points are visible: synthesis of inputs and first-draft generation are strong candidates, but the scoping decision and exception handling require human judgment. Without this decomposition, the PM would have asked AI to 'write a PRD' and gotten generic output that misses the real work.

frameworks.name: Vercel's 'Build It Now' Filter
frameworks.description: A five-criterion checklist for determining whether a workflow is ready for an AI agent deployment today versus deferred to a future architecture.
when_to_apply: We have a list of ten workflows and need to decide which ones get an AI agent first
My team wants to automate a process with an agent but I'm not sure it's the right kind of work for current AI capabilities
I need a quick go/no-go filter before we invest engineering time building an agent for a specific task
We're scoping an AI agent pilot and need to avoid picking a use case that will fail and kill organizational momentum
Someone proposed automating a workflow that feels too open-ended or hard to verify — I need a structured way to say why
principles: The work must be verifiable — checking whether the agent performed correctly requires no heroics
The workflow must be step-wise and bounded — completable in a defined sequence, not open-ended strategy work
The task must be recurring and painful — people describe it as toil, not as valued work
Inputs and outputs must be known — you understand exactly what enters the system and what constitutes good output
A human must remain in the loop — the agent prepares work, a person approves, edits, or rejects it

source_posts.title: Anthropic, Google, and Vercel All Disagree on AI Agents—Here's What Really Matters in 8 Minutes, Plus a Custom Prompt to Figure out YOUR Career with AI Agents

frameworks.example_application: The expense report reconciliation workflow passes all five criteria: output is verifiable against receipts and GL codes, the process follows a fixed sequence (extract → match → flag → post), finance staff universally describe it as soul-crushing toil, inputs are scanned receipts plus policy rules and outputs are approved/flagged line items, and a human already reviews exceptions before posting. This is a build-it-now candidate. By contrast, the 'draft quarterly board narrative' workflow fails on boundedness and verifiability — there's no defined sequence and no one can check correctness without reading the whole thing with strategic context. That one stays manual.

frameworks.name: Agent Strategy Sequencing
frameworks.description: A four-step sequencing framework for progressing from early agent wins to comprehensive agentic infrastructure while avoiding security failures.
when_to_apply: We have budget for AI agents but no clear roadmap for what to build first versus later
Leadership wants a multi-agent orchestration platform but we haven't deployed a single agent yet
Our first agent pilots worked — now we need to figure out how to scale without creating security gaps
Someone proposed giving an autonomous agent broad system access and I need a framework to push back
We're trying to justify investment in agent infrastructure to leadership after some early wins
principles: Start where value is immediately verifiable before building architecture
Orchestration guardrails should be added even to simple early agents — treat agents as identities, not scripts
Proven wins on simple problems justify investment in deeper orchestration
Security cannot be retrofitted — orchestration is the security perimeter and must be considered from the start
Steps cannot be skipped: don't build orchestration platforms before agents exist to orchestrate, but agents cannot scale without orchestration
steps: Step One: Mine Your Back Office — identify work that is verifiable, bounded, recurring, and universally disliked; build agents there first
Step Two: Wrap those agents in lightweight orchestration — assign each agent an identity, define explicit tools and data access, add logging, require human approval for consequential actions
Step Three: Use those wins to justify deeper orchestration work — adopt shared registries, agent operations tracking, multi-agent patterns, and control planes once value is proven

Step Four: Keep high-profile agent misuse cases as a reference point — when someone proposes an autonomous agent with system access and unclear guardrails, use it as a reminder that unguarded orchestration layers will be exploited

source_posts.title: Anthropic, Google, and Vercel All Disagree on AI Agents—Here's What Really Matters in 8 Minutes, Plus a Custom Prompt to Figure out YOUR Career with AI Agents

frameworks.example_application: The team wants to build a multi-agent orchestration platform before they've deployed a single agent in production. That's Step Three work without Step One proof. The right move is to find the most verifiable, bounded back-office task — like reconciling invoice discrepancies or triaging support tickets — ship an agent there with lightweight identity and logging, prove the value, then use that win to justify the orchestration investment. Skipping to platform-building without working agents to orchestrate produces expensive infrastructure nobody trusts and nobody uses.

frameworks.name: Integration Complexity vs. Advantage 2x2 Portfolio Strategy
frameworks.description: A four-quadrant matrix that classifies AI tools by integration complexity and advantage delivered, producing a portfolio sequencing strategy (buy first, pilot with guardrails, committed teams only, or caution) and a recommended budget allocation across tool archetypes.
when_to_apply: We have budget for AI tools but need to decide which to roll out first and which to defer
Leadership is asking for a sequenced AI tool adoption roadmap with clear rationale for prioritization
We piloted several AI tools and now need to decide which ones justify full investment versus staying experimental
Our team is small and we can't absorb more than one complex integration at a time — how do we pick?
I need a portfolio-level view of our AI tool stack to justify budget allocation across tool types
principles: Low complexity, high advantage tools get deployed first without extensive evaluation overhead
Medium complexity, high advantage tools require two-week pilots with defined guardrails and tuning
High complexity, high advantage tools require executive sponsorship and a dedicated senior owner for at least six months — do not start without this
Caution-tier tools (new/unproven or low signal-to-noise) should never be in the core stack unless they graduate to another quadrant
Recommended portfolio allocation: 70% primitives and guardrails, 20% workflow and orchestration, 10% bets on emerging categories
If pricing does not make sense at 10x pilot scale, do not start the pilot

source_posts.title: Grab My Prompt To Help Find the 1% of AI Tools That Actually Work (+50 Tool Reviews to Get Started)

frameworks.example_application: The team's coding assistant falls in the low-complexity/high-advantage quadrant — it plugs into existing IDEs, delivers measurable time savings on day one, and requires no dedicated owner. Buy it now. The AI-driven customer support orchestration platform sits in high-complexity/high-advantage: it touches live customer data, requires CRM integration, and needs prompt tuning per product line. Without an executive sponsor and a senior owner committed for six months, it will stall after the pilot. The trendy 'AI meeting summarizer' startup has no clear pricing model at scale and its advantage signal is weak — it stays in the caution tier and never enters the core stack. Budget allocation: 70% goes to the coding assistant and similar primitives, 20% to the support orchestration pilot, 10% reserved for emerging bets like the summarizer if it graduates.

frameworks.name: Ten-Question Vendor Diligence Protocol
frameworks.description: A set of ten adversarial questions to ask AI tool vendors during serious evaluation that surface operational reality, hidden costs, lock-in risks, and genuine product differentiation faster than standard sales demos.
when_to_apply: We're about to sign an enterprise contract with an AI vendor and I want to stress-test their claims before committing
A vendor's demo looked impressive but I can't tell if there's real IP or just a thin wrapper on an LLM API
I need to evaluate whether an AI tool will actually survive in production or just work in controlled demos
We're comparing three AI vendors and need a consistent set of adversarial questions to surface real differences
Our team is piloting an AI tool and I want to understand our lock-in risk and data portability before we go deeper
principles: Vendors unprepared for these questions reveal their product's production-readiness by their inability to answer
Observable inputs, outputs, eval results, and drift graphs are the minimum bar for a vendor claiming their product works
PII handling hand-waving ('industry best practices') signals the vendor has not thought through data governance
An unusable or missing data export format means you are buying a dependency, not a tool
Vendors who cannot name what broke for their last three churned customers are either too new or dishonest
Median latency is a lie — require P95 latency under realistic traffic shape
Any vendor who claims zero false positives or zero false negatives has miscalibrated their system
A vendor who cannot answer 'what is the cheapest way to get 80% of this value without your product' does not know their own differentiation
steps: Ask: Show me observability — inputs, outputs, eval results, and drift graphs from a real production deployment (not a demo).
Ask: What is your de-identification and PII handling story end-to-end — detection, logging, retention, and access controls?
Ask: How do we export our data, configurations, and memories? Show me a real export file.
Ask: Which parts of this product are your actual IP versus thin wrappers on a model API?
Ask: What broke for your last three churned customers — what was the pattern?
Ask: What is your latency at P95 under our traffic shape?
Ask: What are your false positive and false negative rates on our data after tuning?
Ask: What roadmap items would we have to wait for to meet our requirements?
Ask: Show me your incident response SLA and comms plan, including a real postmortem from an actual outage.
Ask: What is the cheapest way to achieve 80% of this value without buying your product?

source_posts.title: Grab My Prompt To Help Find the 1% of AI Tools That Actually Work (+50 Tool Reviews to Get Started)

frameworks.example_application: The vendor couldn't produce a real export file — they offered 'we can work with your team on that.' That's the tell: there is no export. Combined with their inability to name what broke for churned customers ('we don't really have churn') and their differentiation answer revealing the entire product is a prompt chain on top of GPT-4 with no proprietary model or data layer, this is a thin wrapper selling a dependency. The only genuine signal was their PII handling — they had a real end-to-end story with detection, redaction logs, and retention policies. That's one out of ten. Walk away or negotiate wrapper-level pricing, not platform-level pricing.

frameworks.name: Agency Task Selection Grid
frameworks.description: A two-axis matrix for prioritizing which tasks to delegate to AI agents first, based on potential time savings and task ambiguity/risk, to maximize adoption while minimizing error consequences.
when_to_apply: We have a list of processes we could give to AI agents but don't know which ones to pilot first
Leadership wants to automate high-value knowledge work but I'm worried about error consequences we can't easily detect
Our agent can do a lot of tasks technically, but we need to sequence rollout so users actually trust and adopt it
We're designing a phased AI agent deployment roadmap and need a principled way to prioritize use cases
The team is drawn to automating the hardest, highest-value tasks first — how do I argue for a different starting point?
principles: Time savings alone is not the right optimization dimension for early agentic deployment — verification cost is
Start in the high-savings, low-ambiguity quadrant (e.g., coupon testing, price comparison, document collection) where correctness is immediately visible and error consequences are minimal
High-value tasks are often high-ambiguity tasks where correctness is hard to verify and errors have serious consequences — avoid these early
Tasks where the agent can fully explain its reasoning and the human can quickly validate the result are the safest starting points
Gradually expand to more ambiguous domains only as trust accumulates through supervised experience
Expertise and control are often part of the value in knowledge work — design for augmentation first, full automation second
steps: Map each candidate process onto two axes: potential time savings (x-axis) and ambiguity/risk (y-axis, combining task ambiguity with consequence severity of errors)
Identify the high-savings, low-ambiguity quadrant as the initial deployment zone
For each task in the initial zone, verify the agent can explain its reasoning and the human can quickly validate the result
Deploy in the initial zone and accumulate supervised usage to build user trust and calibrate mental models
After trust is established in the initial zone, evaluate expansion to higher-ambiguity tasks, using verified reliability as the gate — not just capability maturity

source_posts.title: I Sat Down with OpenAI's Head of Engineering for Atlas to Talk Future of Work, the Atlas Browser, and AI Agents—Catch the Exclusive Interview Here

frameworks.example_application: Mapping the procurement team's candidate tasks onto the grid: coupon testing and price comparison land in the high-savings / low-ambiguity quadrant — the agent's output is a number that can be verified against a known source in seconds, and a wrong answer costs a retry, not a contract dispute. Vendor contract negotiation sits in high-savings / high-ambiguity — correctness depends on legal nuance the team can't quickly validate, and an error could lock in unfavorable terms for years. The deployment sequence is clear: start with price comparison to build calibrated trust, then use that supervised track record as the gate for expanding into contract review — not the agent's raw capability score.

frameworks.name: Intelligence Navigator Reframe
frameworks.description: Reframes the AI value shift by arguing that insight generation has become commodity (like cheap TVs) while human judgment and implementation have become scarce (like drywall repair), repositioning where professionals should focus.
when_to_apply: I'm a consultant/analyst and clients are starting to use ChatGPT to do what they used to hire me for
We're trying to figure out how to reprice our advisory services now that AI can generate the same deliverables
Someone on my team said AI will replace knowledge workers because it can synthesize information faster than we can
I need to explain to my organization why we still need experienced humans even though AI produces good-enough analysis
I'm restructuring my career around AI and trying to figure out which of my skills are still worth investing in
principles: Intelligence generation (gathering, analyzing, synthesizing) is now abundant and cheap
Human judgment, implementation, and navigation around insights remain scarce and expensive
Value has migrated from getting TO insight to getting FROM insight to outcome
The bottleneck determines where value lives — identify the new bottleneck, not the old one
Being an 'intelligence navigator' (knowing which insights matter and how to act on them) is non-commodifiable in the near term

source_posts.title: Good Judgement is a Million Dollar Skill in the Age of AI, But No One's Teaching It

frameworks.example_application: The conventional read is that AI threatens this management consulting team because it can produce market analyses in minutes that used to take weeks. That's wrong. The analysis was never the scarce part — the client already had three conflicting reports on their desk before hiring consultants. The value was always in a senior partner walking into a boardroom, knowing which of those analyses to ignore, which political dynamics shaped the data, and how to sequence the implementation so the CFO didn't kill the initiative in Q2. That navigation layer — judgment about which insights matter, in what order, given these specific organizational constraints — is what's actually scarce now, and it's getting scarcer as the volume of generated insight explodes.

frameworks.name: Insight Triage (Curation Practice)
frameworks.description: A structured framework for filtering AI-generated insights by implementability rather than analytical quality, explicitly including deprioritization as a core judgment output.
when_to_apply: AI just gave me twenty recommendations and I need to figure out which three to actually present to leadership
I'm worried that showing all the AI-generated analysis will overwhelm stakeholders and dilute the important findings
A team member keeps surfacing interesting AI-discovered patterns but none of them seem actionable given our current constraints
I need to demonstrate strategic judgment in how I curate and present AI-assisted analysis, not just volume of output
How do I justify to my boss what I chose NOT to pursue from the AI's recommendations?
principles: Curation is more valuable than generation when generation is cheap
Evaluate insights for implementability, not just analytical rigor
Assess political viability given existing stakeholder dynamics
Assess economic meaningfulness given the actual business model
Assess executability given real organizational capacity
Assess timing given current priorities and constraints
Explicit deprioritization (with reasoning) is as important as prioritization — stating what you're NOT doing and why demonstrates judgment
steps: Generate a broad option space of insights using available tools
Evaluate each insight against four implementability filters: political viability, economic meaningfulness, organizational executability, and timing
Select the small number of insights that pass all filters
Explicitly document and explain the insights being deprioritized and why
Present both the selected insights and the deprioritization logic to demonstrate judgment

source_posts.title: Good Judgement is a Million Dollar Skill in the Age of AI, But No One's Teaching It

frameworks.example_application: Out of twelve strategic opportunities the AI surfaced from competitive analysis, only two survive all four filters. The market-adjacency play is analytically elegant but fails political viability — the SVP of Sales has publicly committed to the current vertical focus and reversing that requires capital the team doesn't have. The pricing restructure fails timing — Q4 is three weeks away and the billing system migration is already consuming engineering. Deprioritizing these explicitly, with reasoning, is what separates this from a raw AI output dump. The two survivors — renegotiating the channel partner terms and launching the self-serve tier — pass all four filters and represent the actual action set.

frameworks.name: The Transition Play
frameworks.description: A five-step sequence for shifting from insight-generation work to implementation-and-judgment work, applicable to both external consultants and internal professionals navigating AI commoditization.
when_to_apply: I keep delivering great analyses and recommendations but AI tools are making that same output available to everyone — how do I stay valuable?
I'm an internal strategist or consultant and I realize my career capital is built on insight generation, not demonstrated judgment
I want to shift from being known as someone who produces smart analysis to someone who delivers measurable business outcomes
My consulting practice is built on deliverables (decks, reports, models) that AI can now approximate — I need a repositioning plan
I have strong analytical skills but no visible track record of owning complete outcomes end-to-end
principles: Audit current time allocation — if more than 30% goes to insight generation, you are over-indexed on the commodifying part
Demonstrate judgment through complete outcomes, not just insights or analysis
Document reasoning and decision logic, not just execution steps
Make outcomes visible to the people who matter with business impact framing
Repetition builds credibility — one outcome is luck, three is a pattern, five is a practice
steps: Audit your current work to measure what percentage goes to insight generation vs. implementation — flag if generation exceeds 30%
Select one painful, visible, measurable problem and commit to delivering a complete outcome (working system or changed state), not just a recommendation
Document not just what you did but how you thought: what made the problem worth solving, how you prioritized it, what constraints shaped your approach, and what you would do differently
Make the outcome visible to relevant stakeholders, framing around business impact rather than technical achievement
Repeat until you have at least three similar outcomes that establish a recognizable pattern of judgment

source_posts.title: Good Judgement is a Million Dollar Skill in the Age of AI, But No One's Teaching It

frameworks.example_application: After auditing time allocation, 55% of weekly hours go to producing analyses and recommendations that stakeholders increasingly generate themselves with AI tools. The first transition move: take the recurring inventory optimization problem that costs the ops team $200K/quarter in excess stock, and instead of delivering another recommendation deck, own the outcome — build the working reorder system, get it live, measure the savings. Document not just the system but the reasoning: why this problem over three others, why the threshold was set at 14 days not 7, what tradeoff was accepted on stockout risk. After three such delivered outcomes with visible business impact, the pattern reads as 'this person solves expensive problems end-to-end' rather than 'this person produces good analysis.'

frameworks.name: Production-to-Problem-Solving Spectrum
frameworks.description: A spectrum that distinguishes AI-replaceable production work from AI-augmented problem-solving work, used to help junior professionals reposition their value.
when_to_apply: I'm a junior professional and my deliverables are starting to look like something ChatGPT could produce — how do I stay relevant?
My manager keeps assigning me templated execution tasks and I can't figure out how to demonstrate strategic thinking
I'm a manager trying to figure out which junior roles on my team are actually at risk of being automated away
I want to use AI to 10x my output but I'm worried that just makes me a more efficient version of something that gets eliminated
I'm preparing for a performance review and need to show I bring judgment, not just output
principles: Pure production work (executing defined tasks, following templates) is AI-replaceable
Problem-solving work (framing ambiguous problems, identifying what needs to be built) is AI-augmented
Organizations are not set up to push juniors rightward on the spectrum — individuals must do this themselves
Reframing tasks to surface the underlying business question demonstrates problem-solving ability
If stuck in production mode, 10-20x productivity via AI buys time to develop problem-solving skills
steps: Identify whether your current work is framed as production (produce this, run this, build this) or problem-solving
Reframe each task by asking: what business question is this answering, and is this the right format?
Bring options and alternatives rather than a single output
Explicitly communicate the 'why' behind your work, not just the 'what'
If unable to escape production framing, demonstrate 10-20x AI productivity to buy time

source_posts.title: I've Talked to Hundreds of Companies About AI & Jobs: Here's The Jobs Guide No One is Writing (+ Prompts)

frameworks.example_application: This analyst's daily work — pulling data, formatting slides, running standard models — sits firmly on the production end of the spectrum. The tell: every task arrives pre-framed ('build this deck,' 'run this analysis'), and the output is evaluated on speed and format compliance, not on whether it answered the right question. The move is to start reframing: instead of delivering the requested churn report, come back with 'I ran the churn numbers, but the real signal is that our highest-LTV segment is churning at 2x the rate of everyone else — here are three hypotheses why and what I'd test next.' That shifts the visible contribution from production to problem-solving, and it's the only version of this work that survives AI doing the production layer at near-zero cost.

frameworks.name: Domain-vs-Skills Matrix
frameworks.description: A two-axis matrix contrasting domain expertise against skill level to help mid-career professionals identify where their durable competitive advantage lies in an AI-commoditized skills landscape.
when_to_apply: I have 10+ years in my field and I'm wondering whether my experience still matters or if a junior with ChatGPT can do what I do
I'm considering a career pivot to a completely different industry and trying to figure out how much of my value I'd leave on the table
A hiring manager asked me what I bring that AI doesn't, and I didn't have a clear answer
I'm good at my domain but feel like my technical skills are outdated — should I invest in upskilling or double down on domain depth?
I'm tempted to start over in a hot field like AI/ML but I've spent years building expertise in healthcare operations
principles: Pre-AI, career advancement required developing both skills and domain expertise in parallel
Post-AI, skills are commoditized — AI can teach and execute skills; it cannot replicate accumulated domain experience
Domain expertise (pattern recognition, stakeholder relationships, institutional knowledge, project scar tissue) is the primary moat for mid-career professionals
Abandoning domain expertise entirely is high-risk; adjacent hops that carry existing domain credit are safer
AI proficiency must be actively socialized — share prompts, teach decomposition, demonstrate output verification, build reusable frameworks

source_posts.title: I've Talked to Hundreds of Companies About AI & Jobs: Here's The Jobs Guide No One is Writing (+ Prompts)

frameworks.example_application: A senior supply chain manager considering a pivot into product management at a tech company is carrying fifteen years of vendor negotiation patterns, supplier relationship capital, and crisis triage instincts that no AI can replicate. The skills gap (product frameworks, user story writing, roadmap tooling) is exactly what AI commoditizes — learnable in weeks with AI assistance. The domain expertise is the irreplaceable asset. A full pivot into, say, fintech product management would abandon that entire moat. The higher-value move is an adjacent hop: supply chain SaaS, logistics tech, or procurement platforms — domains where that scar tissue transfers and the new skills layer on top rather than replace what's underneath.

frameworks.name: Grace Period Hypothesis
frameworks.description: Reframes the senior professional's AI challenge not as a threat requiring immediate expertise, but as a temporary window of organizational tolerance that rewards leading with strategic judgment while acquiring AI skills.
when_to_apply: I'm a senior leader applying for roles and I'm not sure whether to emphasize my domain expertise or scramble to get AI credentials
Our hiring committee is debating whether to pass on a strong senior candidate because they don't have AI experience on their resume
