Score yourself on D-T-R honestly before scoring the giant
Giants automatically get T=5 and R=5; their D score depends on their existing distribution channels
Your defensible beachhead is only the lever where you still outscore them
Speed without exclusivity is acceleration into a wall
Pivot the roadmap — not the pitch deck — when advantage shrinks
steps: Step 1 — Give yourself a brutally honest D-T-R score: rate your Distribution (user activation without vendor approval), Tokenization (fraction of raw data that is model-ready), and Reward Clarity (auto-gradable success) each on a 1–5 scale
Step 2 — Clone the giant's likely score: assign T=5 and R=5 to the hyperscaler by default, and estimate their realistic Distribution score based on existing channel embeds
Step 3 — Circle the lever where you still outscore them: identify the single D, T, or R dimension where you have a structural advantage

Step 4 — Design a moat-widening sprint: define what you can ship in 90 days to make that lever at least twice as hard to copy (e.g., lock a design partner, deploy edge devices, collect a proprietary reward dataset)
Step 5 — Schedule a re-test trigger: re-run the test quarterly or whenever a major platform files about your vertical; if your advantage shrinks, pivot the roadmap

source_posts.title: We killed your startup, lol—what to build when Sam Altman keeps shipping better models

frameworks.example_application: This startup's D-T-R scores are D=4 (embedded in 200 dental clinics via hardware), T=2 (using generic medical NLP), R=3 (decent outcome labels). The giant's scores: D=2 (no dental channel), T=5, R=5. The surviving lever is Distribution — the physical clinic integration. But T=2 means the product's data pipeline is trivially replicable once a giant partners with a dental SaaS. The 90-day sprint must lock exclusive data-sharing agreements with those 200 clinics and deploy edge inference on-prem, converting distribution access into a proprietary tokenization asset. Without that, the D=4 advantage decays to commodity within two platform update cycles.

frameworks.name: Mountain Pass Scouting Framework
frameworks.description: A three-question scouting method for identifying market niches where structural friction in distribution, data tokenization, or reward clarity makes the terrain too costly for hyperscalers to dominate, paired with a five-test field checklist to confirm the pass is real.
when_to_apply: I have a startup idea in a vertical but I'm worried OpenAI or Google will just ship this as a feature — how do I know if the niche is actually safe?
We're choosing between two industry verticals to build our AI product in and need to figure out which one has real structural friction versus just being underserved temporarily
An investor asked me why a hyperscaler can't replicate what we're building in six months and I don't have a rigorous answer
I'm looking at a messy, regulated industry and trying to figure out if the messiness is a moat or just a sign the market isn't worth entering
My co-founder wants to build a general-purpose AI tool but I think we should go narrow and vertical — I need a framework to evaluate which verticals are actually defensible
principles: Hyperscalers hesitate where data is messy, compliance is thorny, or reward loops require specialist human judgment
A valid mountain pass must have at least one D-T-R lever that is structurally hard for a hyperscaler (D<3, T≤2, or R≤2)
The sector TAM should be large enough to matter (e.g., >$500M) but the wedge small enough for a tiny team to ship fast
Answering 'yes' to any two of the three scouting questions signals defensible terrain
If the map stays flat (no friction answers), keep walking — don't build on open plains
steps: Ask the Distribution Friction question: Where do decision-makers sit behind fragmented channels, procurement hoops, or political approval?
Ask the Data Stubbornness question: Which critical inputs refuse to convert to clean text — sensors, proprietary file formats, photo or thermal blends?
Ask the Outcome Ambiguity question: Where does quality still require a licensed human to approve — IRB boards, underwriters, compliance officers?

If two or more answers are 'yes,' run the five-test field checklist: Channel Test (domain warm intros required), Converter Test (30%+ of raw data fails without custom ETL), Oracle Test (removing licensed reviewer drops accuracy below tolerance), Token-Shock Test (10x cheaper model barely dents your price), Exit-Clause Test (customer cannot swap to a hyperscaler in <30 days without retraining or refiling)

source_posts.title: We killed your startup, lol—what to build when Sam Altman keeps shipping better models

frameworks.example_application: The pass is real for this veterinary radiology AI startup. Distribution friction is high — every clinic buys through a different practice management vendor with unique integrations, and the buying committee includes a practice owner who barely checks email. Data stubbornness is severe — the core inputs are DICOM thermal overlays from eight different ultrasound machines, and 30%+ of raw scans fail without custom ETL. Outcome ambiguity is locked in — a board-certified veterinary radiologist must sign off on every diagnosis for malpractice reasons. That's three out of three scouting questions answered yes. Running the field checklist confirms it: Token-Shock Test passes because a 10x cheaper foundation model doesn't change the $85 per-read price driven by specialist review costs, and the Exit-Clause Test passes because switching requires re-filing with state veterinary boards and retraining on clinic-specific DICOM pipelines — that's a 90+ day migration, not a weekend swap.

frameworks.name: Three Bottleneck Framework (Compute, Context, Integration)
frameworks.description: Classifies the root cause of AI tool frustration into exactly one of three constraint types, enabling targeted plan upgrades rather than indiscriminate spending.
when_to_apply: I'm hitting limits on my AI tool and I'm not sure if I need a bigger plan or a different tool entirely
I keep copy-pasting data between my apps and ChatGPT and the whole workflow feels broken
My AI chat keeps forgetting what I said earlier in long sessions and I'm wondering if upgrading will fix that
I'm comparing AI subscription tiers and the feature differences all sound the same — I can't tell which one solves my actual problem
I'm paying for multiple AI tools and suspect I'm solving the same problem twice with none of them doing it well
principles: Every AI failure traces to one primary bottleneck: Compute (how many heavy requests you get), Context (how much content the model can hold at once), or Integration (proximity of AI to your data and tools)
Pay to lift the bottleneck that actually blocks you; paying for anything else adds cost without unlocking value
Fix Integration first when multiple bottlenecks appear — moving AI next to your data often eliminates perceived compute and context pain
Compute pain is time-of-day sensitive (vanishes at off-peak hours); context pain is document-size sensitive; integration pain is workflow-topology sensitive
Each pricing tier is designed to relieve one specific constraint — identify which constraint matches your problem before choosing a tier
steps: Observe your AI friction for one day: tally each complaint under C (compute), Cx (context), or In (integration)
Check compute: Did you wait for a capacity timer this week? If yes, compute is your bottleneck
Check context: Did you split a file into parts or lose chat memory mid-session? If yes, context is your bottleneck
Check integration: Did copy-paste steal more than 10 minutes a day? If yes, integration is your bottleneck
Match your identified bottleneck to the vendor tier that specifically addresses it using the compute-context-integration grid
Apply the ROI formula: (hourly rate × hours saved per month) ÷ monthly plan cost — upgrade only if result exceeds 2×, lock in at 4×

source_posts.title: You Will Choose Wisely: The Definitive Guide to Picking (and Paying for) an AI Plan in Q2 2025

frameworks.example_application: The frustration here is context, not compute. The user keeps splitting long contracts into chunks and losing prior conversation history mid-analysis — that's document-size sensitivity, not rate-limit pain. Upgrading to a plan with more API calls per hour would waste money; the fix is a tier (or tool) that extends the context window. Before even spending on that, though, check integration: if they're copy-pasting those contract chunks from a document management system into ChatGPT manually, moving to Copilot embedded in their existing workflow might dissolve the context pain entirely by keeping the AI next to the source files.

frameworks.name: AI Subscription ROI Quick-Math
frameworks.description: A simple formula and threshold system for deciding whether to keep, upgrade, or cancel an AI subscription based on time-value return.
when_to_apply: I'm paying for ChatGPT Plus, Claude Pro, and Copilot and I'm not sure which ones are actually worth it
My AI subscription just raised prices and I need to decide if the new cost is still justified
The project that made me subscribe to this AI tool is over and I'm not sure I still need it
I'm considering upgrading from a free tier to a paid AI plan and want to know if the math works
It's end of quarter and I want a quick sanity check on whether my AI tool spending makes sense
principles: ROI = (hourly rate × hours saved per month) ÷ monthly plan cost
Below 2× ROI: downgrade or cancel
Between 2× and 4× ROI: keep but re-evaluate next quarter
Above 4× ROI: lock in; consider switching to annual billing
Re-run the test every quarter because GPU prices fall and context windows expand, changing the denominator and numerator over time
steps: Estimate your effective hourly rate (billing rate for professionals, or time-value estimate for others)
Track hours saved per month attributable to the specific plan
Divide (hourly rate × hours saved) by the monthly plan cost
Compare the result to the 2×/4× thresholds to make the keep/cancel/upgrade decision
Repeat the calculation each quarter

source_posts.title: You Will Choose Wisely: The Definitive Guide to Picking (and Paying for) an AI Plan in Q2 2025

frameworks.example_application: The ChatGPT Pro subscription at $200/month scores 1.4× ROI. At a $150/hour effective rate, it's saving roughly 1.9 hours per month — but the Plus plan at $20/month covers 90% of the same use cases and would score 10×+ ROI on even a single hour saved. The right move isn't canceling AI entirely; it's downgrading to Plus and redirecting the $180/month difference. The Pro-exclusive features (extended thinking, higher rate limits) sound compelling but aren't hitting real workflow hours.

frameworks.name: AI Resume Failure Catalog (9 Categories)
frameworks.description: An enumerated taxonomy of the nine most common ways AI experience is misrepresented or undersold on resumes, each with distinguishing signals.
when_to_apply: I've listed AI tools and projects on my resume but I'm not getting callbacks and I can't figure out why
I'm reviewing a candidate's resume and their AI experience feels impressive but I can't tell what they actually did
I helped build an AI feature at work but I'm not sure how to describe my specific contribution without overclaiming or underclaiming
My resume mentions GPT, LangChain, and RAG but a mentor told me it reads like a buzzword list
I did real AI work but it was a side project, not enterprise-scale — how do I present it without inflating it?
principles: Vague observers describe interest or curiosity without any evidence of application
Tool-dumpers list names without explaining the problem solved or outcome achieved
Inflated generalists use enterprise-scale language for individual or side projects
Undersold real workers did valuable things but described them too generically to be legible
Generic contributors use soft verbs like 'collaborated' without specifying their actual contribution
Buzzword blenders stack jargon to sound technical without clarifying what the AI actually did
Over-owners claim sole credit for team work, which breaks trust in interviews
Disconnected wins cite business outcomes without explaining what role AI played
Prompt-as-product illusionists frame a one-off manual prompt as a shipped product

source_posts.title: The AI Resume Survival Guide (for 2025 and Beyond)

frameworks.example_application: The active failure mode is 'disconnected wins.' The bullet reads 'Drove 30% increase in customer retention using AI-powered analytics' — but there's no trace of what the AI actually did, what model or tool was involved, or what the candidate's role was in building versus consuming it. The business outcome is real but completely decoupled from any legible AI contribution. The fix isn't removing the metric — it's inserting the mechanism: what AI system, what it did, and what this person specifically built or configured to make it work.

frameworks.name: AI-Assisted Resume Refinement Process
frameworks.description: A four-step process for using AI tools to improve resume bullets without losing authenticity, specificity, or the author's voice.
when_to_apply: I pasted my resume into ChatGPT and everything came back sounding like corporate word soup
I know what I did at work but I can't figure out how to make it sound impressive without lying
I want to tailor the same experience for different job postings without rewriting from scratch each time
I'm preparing for interviews and want to identify the narrative threads across my resume bullets
I'm worried my AI-polished resume will get flagged as generic or trigger AI detection concerns
principles: AI is a writing coach, not a ghostwriter — it needs tight input to produce useful output
Start with honest, unpolished substance before giving anything to an AI tool
Constrained, specific prompts produce better results than open-ended ones like 'make this better'
Use AI to generate optionality (multiple framings) then select and polish manually
The final voice must remain the author's — AI should sharpen, not replace, human expression
Never let AI fabricate outcomes or metrics you did not actually achieve
steps: Write out what you actually did in plain, honest language — no polish, no performance, just the real description as you'd explain it to a colleague
Give the AI tool specific, constrained instructions naming the desired output format, the role context, and explicit requirements (tool used, task completed, measurable outcome, appropriate tone)
Ask the AI to generate 2–3 alternate framings of the same content (e.g., one more technical, one more impact-focused) to find the best fit for the target role
Use the AI reflectively: feed in multiple bullets and ask it to identify themes, patterns, or what they reveal about how you work — use this for narrative summaries and interview prep

source_posts.title: The AI Resume Survival Guide (for 2025 and Beyond)

frameworks.example_application: The raw input is 'I built a dashboard in Looker that the sales team used to track pipeline.' Step one produced honest substance. Step two constrains the AI: 'Rewrite this as a resume bullet for a data analyst role. Include the tool (Looker), the task (pipeline visibility for sales), and a measurable outcome (reduced weekly reporting time by 3 hours). Use a direct, non-corporate tone.' Step three generates three framings — one technical ('Designed and deployed a Looker dashboard integrating CRM data...'), one impact-focused ('Eliminated 3 hours/week of manual reporting for a 12-person sales team...'), one hybrid. The technical version fits the target role best but the impact framing surfaces a theme — this person consistently builds self-serve tools that remove bottlenecks. That theme, identified in step four, becomes the backbone of the summary section and a ready-made interview narrative.

frameworks.name: AI Detector Risk Mitigation Checklist
frameworks.description: A structured set of checks and interventions to reduce the probability that a resume is falsely flagged as AI-generated by automated screening tools, by diagnosing low-perplexity and low-burstiness signals.
when_to_apply: I used ChatGPT to help write my resume and I'm worried it reads like AI wrote it
I ran my resume through an AI detector and it came back flagged — how do I fix it without starting over?
My resume bullets all sound the same — polished but generic — and I'm applying to companies that use automated screening
I want to make sure my resume sounds like me and not like averaged professional prose
Every bullet on my resume follows the same structure and uses words like 'leveraged' and 'utilized'
principles: AI detectors flag predictability (low a search-augmented model) and uniformity (low burstiness), not actual AI use
Overly polished, safe writing scores worse on these metrics than messy, varied human writing
Never paste AI-generated text directly into a resume — always rewrite in your own words
Verb choice is a key signal: tactile, specific verbs (rebuilt, debugged, scrapped) score better than safe ones (leveraged, utilized, enhanced)
Sentence rhythm variation — mixing short punchy phrases with longer complex clauses — increases burstiness
A little imperfection builds credibility; perfect polish raises suspicion
Re-exposing yourself to pre-AI human writing (old blogs, essays, novels) helps recalibrate your natural voice
steps: Run the final resume draft through a publicly available text-classification tool before submitting
Identify which sections scored lowest on a search-augmented model or burstiness
Check for structural repetition: are multiple bullets following the same 'Built X using Y to achieve Z' pattern?
Replace safe, generic verbs (leveraged, utilized, developed, enhanced) with verbs that reflect real action and struggle (rebuilt, debugged, restructured, scrapped, retrained)
Vary sentence rhythm deliberately: mix short fragments with longer, winding clauses; break uniform pacing
Rewrite any AI-drafted sections in your own voice before finalizing

source_posts.title: The AI Resume Survival Guide (for 2025 and Beyond)

frameworks.example_application: The resume scores 87% AI-likelihood. The problem is concentrated in the experience section: every bullet follows 'Leveraged X to enhance Y, resulting in Z% improvement' — identical syntactic structure, safe verbs, no variation in sentence length. Replacing 'leveraged' with 'rebuilt,' 'enhanced' with 'overhauled,' breaking two bullets into short fragments ('Scrapped the old pipeline. Started over.'), and varying clause length drops the score to 31%. The perplexity issue was structural repetition, not content quality.

frameworks.name: AI Leverage Map
frameworks.description: A classification of three structural positions where AI can create compounding competitive advantage, used to diagnose where a company actually has strategic leverage.
when_to_apply: We have multiple AI initiatives running but can't articulate why any of them are defensible
Our AI roadmap feels like a list of features rather than a coherent strategic position
We're debating whether our advantage is in our data, our integrations, or our understanding of the user problem
A competitor just shipped a similar AI feature and leadership is panicking — I need to explain why our position is or isn't at risk
We're trying to decide whether to invest in acquiring users, building better AI infrastructure, or going deeper into domain-specific workflows
principles: Advantage in the AI era comes from distribution, middleware, or workflow—not model access
These three positions are distinct but interdependent: distribution provides data, middleware converts data into behavior, workflow is where value is delivered
A strategy must be anchored in at least one of the three or it is merely a wish

Distribution advantage = existing user surfaces and trust; Middleware advantage = ability to turn model output into reliable system behavior; Workflow advantage = deep knowledge of user friction points

source_posts.title: You Don't Need Better Models—You Need a Better Strategy

frameworks.example_application: This company's AI play sits entirely in the middleware layer — they've built reliable orchestration that turns noisy model output into consistent, auditable decisions for regulated industries. That's real. But they have no distribution advantage: they're selling through partners who own the customer relationship and the data feedback loop. The workflow layer is also thin — they're operating on generic templates, not deep domain-specific friction knowledge. The strategic move isn't to improve model quality; it's to acquire a distribution surface (even a narrow one) so the middleware advantage compounds through proprietary data instead of decaying as competitors replicate the orchestration patterns.

frameworks.name: AI Strategy Kernel
frameworks.description: An adaptation of Rumelt's diagnosis-guiding policy-coherent action framework applied specifically to AI product strategy, forcing teams to narrow focus and build compounding leverage rather than scattered features.
when_to_apply: We have a dozen AI features in flight and no principled way to decide which ones to keep funding
Our AI roadmap changes every time a new model drops — we need a strategy that's durable across capability shifts
We're shipping AI that gets good reactions in demos but isn't creating any compounding advantage
Leadership wants to go from scattered AI experiments to a coherent AI product strategy with clear bets
Our AI initiative has lots of activity and launches but feels like it's not building toward anything
principles: Diagnosis narrows the problem space by identifying where leverage actually exists, not what is theoretically possible
Guiding policy is a directional filter—a posture about what game you are playing—not a roadmap or feature list
Coherent actions reinforce one another and compound over time; disconnected AI features do not constitute a strategy
Start with the smallest possible wedge that fits the guiding policy and creates a feedback loop
Kill features that don't compound leverage, regardless of how well they demo
Treat strategy as a repeating loop, not a one-time planning exercise
steps: Diagnose your leverage position: Map your business honestly against distribution, middleware, and workflow to identify where you have an unfair advantage in deploying AI
Set a guiding policy: Articulate a posture that commits to one or more leverage positions and explicitly rules out directions that don't fit—this acts as a filter for all future decisions
Identify coherent actions: Choose a thin starting wedge aligned to the guiding policy, then sequence subsequent builds so each reinforces the last and creates a feedback loop
Observe system behavior: Watch deployed AI tools in production, collect signals, and use findings to sharpen middleware, UX, prompts, and fallback logic
Repeat the loop: Revisit diagnosis regularly (at least quarterly), recommit to or explicitly update the guiding policy, and ship new wedges that reflect current learning

source_posts.title: You Don't Need Better Models—You Need a Better Strategy

frameworks.example_application: The team has shipped an AI summarizer, an AI classifier, and an AI chatbot across three different product surfaces in six months. None share data, none feed each other, and none have created switching costs. The diagnosis reveals the real leverage is in the proprietary workflow data flowing through the middleware layer — not in any individual AI feature. The guiding policy becomes: every AI capability must plug into and enrich the shared workflow graph. The chatbot stays because it generates structured interaction data that improves the classifier. The summarizer gets killed — it demos well but operates on public documents and compounds nothing. The next wedge is a feedback loop where classifier corrections from users retrain the model weekly, making the middleware layer progressively harder to replicate.

frameworks.name: AI Execution Architecture Audit
frameworks.description: Four structured questions to determine whether an organization's structure can actually execute an AI strategy, surfacing ownership gaps, quality blind spots, and iteration bottlenecks.
when_to_apply: We have a solid AI strategy but teams keep stepping on each other and nothing compounds
AI features ship once and then never meaningfully improve — they just sit there
Nobody can tell me who actually decides whether an AI feature is working or should be killed
Our AI quality conversations go in circles because everyone has a different definition of 'good enough'
The feedback loop from users back into model improvement feels impossibly slow given our org structure
principles: Most AI strategy failures are architectural, not intellectual—the structure doesn't support the strategy
Ownership of AI experimentation must be distinct from ownership of AI infrastructure
Quality evaluation for AI requires a different mental model than traditional QA because outputs are probabilistic
Iteration speed is a strategic variable; waterfall delivery structures are incompatible with AI compounding
Without a named decision-maker and clear criteria, failed AI features persist and erode trust
steps: Ask: Who owns AI experiments—specifically, who is trusted to put model-backed features in front of users and close the loop back into product?
Ask: Who judges quality and how—what shared language and benchmarks exist for evaluating AI feature performance in production?
Ask: How fast can you close the feedback loop—are UX patterns designed to generate useful signals and can the team act on them without a full rewrite?
Ask: When do you kill something—who owns the call and what criteria trigger it?

source_posts.title: You Don't Need Better Models—You Need a Better Strategy

frameworks.example_application: The strategy doc is sharp — embed AI across three product surfaces — but the audit exposes the real problem. Nobody owns the experiments end-to-end: the ML team builds models, product defines requirements, and engineering deploys, but no single person is trusted to put a model-backed feature in front of users and close the loop. Quality evaluation is ad hoc — the team has no shared language for 'good enough' probabilistic output, so every review cycle turns into a taste debate. The feedback loop takes six weeks because UX wasn't designed to generate usable signals, and retraining requires a full sprint. Two AI features launched eight months ago are still live despite poor engagement because no one has the authority or criteria to kill them. The strategy isn't the problem — the execution architecture has four structural fractures that guarantee drift.

frameworks.name: The Seven Tech Workflows
frameworks.description: A classification system that decomposes any knowledge work job into seven recurring workflow motions, enabling workers to identify where AI provides leverage and where human judgment remains irreplaceable.
when_to_apply: I want to use AI tools at work but I'm not sure which parts of my job they'd actually improve versus just add noise
My team is adopting Copilot/ChatGPT and we need to figure out where to point it first for maximum impact
I'm trying to explain to my manager why my role still matters even though AI can produce drafts of most of my deliverables
We have friction in how work moves through our team and I want to understand whether it's a people problem or a workflow design problem before layering AI on top
I keep hearing 'AI will replace knowledge workers' and I want a concrete way to audit which parts of my job are actually vulnerable
principles: Your job is not your title or output — it is a set of recurring workflow motions
AI amplifies clean, intentional motion and multiplies confusion in messy, unexamined motion
The parts of each workflow that are hardest to describe or tokenize are the parts most resistant to AI replacement (Polanyian tacit knowledge)
Each workflow has a distinct leverage point where AI can extend human capability without replacing judgment
Task thinking is a trap; designing the motion is the new competitive advantage
